sens: State of that which is dead or lifeless
Action of dying or causing death
State of non-functioning or inertia of a part of the body
G3500.detail:
1. The word simply describes the state of that which is dead, the absence of life. In Romans 4:19, Abraham "did not consider that his body was already dead" — this is the image of an aging body, becoming almost inert, incapable of conceiving children: it is a kind of partial death of the body.

2. The word can also refer to the act or process of dying, the act of killing. This is the meaning of the verb from which it comes (nekroô = to make die).

3. In biblical texts, the word takes on a spiritual significance: in 2 Corinthians 4:10, Paul speaks of "bearing in our body the death of Jesus." This is not a literal death, but sharing in the sufferings of Christ, dying to oneself so that Christ may live in us. It is a mystical death, a death to sin and to self.
G3500.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb nekroô, which literally means "to make die" or "to render dead." It is constructed from nekros (dead, corpse). The suffix -sis forms a noun denoting a state or process. This Greek word often translates the Hebrew mâvet (death) in the Greek Old Testament.
G3500.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Greek New Testament. In Romans 4:19, it describes the physical state of Abraham, whose body was aged and barren — a partial death, an incapacity of the body. In 2 Corinthians 4:10, Paul uses the same word to speak of the death of Christ that we bear in our bodies: he evokes suffering, self-denial, sharing in the tribulations of Jesus. The meaning thus shifts from the physical to the spiritual and mystical.
G3500.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that following Jesus involves a death to self, a willingness to suffer and to renounce as Christ did. It is not a morbid or nihilistic death, but a liberating death: by dying to ourselves, we allow the life of Christ to manifest in us. This is the essence of the paschal mystery applied to the life of the disciple.

sens: Recently created, made, or acquired; of little age
Having little time to live, at the beginning of its life
Replacing something old or worn out
Fresh, not yet used or decayed
Recent, contemporary, just occurred
G3501.detail:
1. The primary meaning is temporal: what is new has just appeared, in contrast to the old. The new wine of Matthew 9:17 has not yet fermented for long; it is wine that has just been made, which has not yet stabilized. It is distinguished from old wine, established and stable.

2. The word applies to one who is young in age, at the beginning of their life. The younger son of the parable (Luke 15:13) is referred to as "the young son": he is a young man in terms of age. Similarly, the "young men" of Acts 5:6 are young men in the prime of life.

3. The word also describes what is new, which replaces the old. The "new man" of Colossians 3:10 is the renewed being in Christ, who leaves behind the old nature. The "new covenant" (when the Greek word is νέος) evokes the covenant recently established in contrast to the old.

4. What is new is also what has not yet been used, which is intact. The new wineskins of Luke 5:38 have not yet been stretched by fermentation; they are supple and can hold the new wine without tearing.
G3501.origine: The word νέος comes from an ancient Greek root meaning "to grow" or "to be young." In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it often translates the Hebrew נַעַר (naïar, "young boy") and חָדָשׁ (hadash, "new," "fresh"). The comparative form νεώτερος ("younger," "junior") frequently appears in the epistles to designate young believers in relation to the elders (πρεσβύτεροι). Greek distinguishes νέος (new in time, recent) from καινός (new in quality, original, without previous example) — an important nuance in the New Testament.
G3501.emploi: The word νέος appears 21 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the pastoral epistles. For the meaning "new" (temporal): the new wine (Matthew 9:17, Mark 2:22, Luke 5:37-39) is the image of a fermentation in progress, of a dynamic life that cannot be contained in old wineskins. The new man (Colossians 3:10) and the new covenant (Hebrews 12:24) express renewal in Christ. For the meaning "young": the word designates age or youth — the younger son (Luke 15:12-13), the young men (Acts 5:6), the young widows (1 Timothy 5:11). The comparison νεώτερος often marks the opposition with πρεσβύτεροι ("the elders"), structuring the generational relationship in the church.
G3501.portee: Understanding this distinction between new and old helps grasp the message of the Gospels: the new wine of the Kingdom cannot be poured into old religious structures that would contain it. Jesus announces a living, overflowing reality that requires the new — new wineskins, a new heart. For the believer, "putting on the new man" (Colossians 3:10) is not a superficial addition, but a radical renewal of life and thought in relation to Christ.

sens: A very young bird, still in the nest or shortly after fledging
A small bird, notably a squab or a young dove
Figuratively: that which is young, fragile, tender
G3502.detail:
1. The word concretely designates a bird at an early stage of its life, still dependent. In Luke 2:24, it is the term used for the "young pigeons" that Joseph and Mary offer at the temple: these are not adult birds, but chicks that are easier to procure.
2. It is therefore also a small bird in practical terms: less expensive than an adult, more suitable for a sin offering. Jewish law accepted these young birds for worship (see Leviticus 12:8).
3. The word can also figuratively evoke the idea of fragility, youth, dependence, although this figurative use is not documented in the provided verses.
G3502.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that evokes the idea of novelty and youth (related to the Greek νεος, "new," and νεος, "young"). In the Greek translation of the Old Testament (LXX), it often translates the Hebrew ben, which primarily means "son" but also more broadly "young of" or "young one of." It is a classical word in ancient Greek, well established in everyday language and in religious texts.
G3502.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 2:24. In this passage of the presentation narrative at the temple, it is the exact term used to designate the "young pigeons" that Mary and Joseph offer as a sacrifice, in accordance with the Mosaic law. The context indicates that it is an offering of poverty, as young birds cost less than adults. This choice of vocabulary highlights the humility of Jesus' family.
G3502.portee: This detail informs the reader about the actual conditions of Jesus' birth: his family, though holy, was poor and strictly observed the Law. The offering of young birds shows that even the beginnings of Christ on earth bore the mark of ordinary humanity, with its material limitations. It is an invitation to see how God comes in fragility and humble condition.

sens: the age or period of life when one is young
the state or condition of being a young person
the total years of formation and inexperience before adulthood
the vigor and strength characteristic of young years
G3503.detail:
1. Youth is primarily the stage of life that extends from childhood to adulthood, the time when one is young. It is at this age that the rich young man in Mark 10:20 claims to have "kept all these things from my youth."
2. The word also refers to the condition or state of being young — both the phase of life and what it means for the individual. Timothy is exhorted in 1 Timothy 4:12: "Let no one despise your youth," meaning your position as a young man, your lack of experience, or your unimposing appearance.
3. Youth is the period of moral and spiritual learning and formation. Paul recounts in Acts 26:4 that his life "from the earliest times of my youth" took place in Jerusalem: it is the time when one is shaped, when one acquires convictions.
4. By extension, the word can evoke the freshness, vitality, and natural strength of this age, in contrast to maturity or old age.
G3503.origine: The word νεότης comes from the adjective νέος (néos), which means "young" or "new." The root expresses the idea of what is recent, fresh, full of life. In Hebrew, the Hebrew word נָעוּר (naoûr, "youth") — used mainly in the Greek Old Testament — shares the same reality: the period when a young man or young woman grows and gains strength.
G3503.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels and the early Acts. In the first three occurrences (Matthew 19:20, Mark 10:20, Luke 18:21), it refers to the childhood or youth of the rich young man who claims to have kept the commandments since his youth. In Acts 26:4, Paul uses this word to describe the beginning of his own life. Finally, in 1 Timothy 4:12, Paul encourages Timothy not to let anyone despise his youth, suggesting that youth can be a social handicap or a reason for lack of respect. The context shows that youth is often associated with inexperience or a lack of apparent authority.
G3503.portee: This word reminds the reader that youth is not an excuse, but a reality to be lived with integrity. Paul's call to Timothy — not to let anyone despise his youth, but to make it a strength through example — encourages young Christians to engage their lives without waiting for maturity in age. It is also an invitation to remember that our young years, with their choices and learnings, shape our entire spiritual existence.

sens: Newly planted plant
Person recently converted
Inexperienced or fragile believer in their faith
G3504.detail: 1. In its primary sense, the word refers to a plant that has just been planted in the ground: the image is one of youth and fragility. 2. The Bible uses it figuratively to speak of a person who has recently converted to the Christian faith. This is someone who has just been spiritually born, who is starting in the Christian life. 3. The word emphasizes inexperience and vulnerability: it is a believer who is still weak, who has not had time to take root and mature in their relationship with God (1 Timothy 3:6).
G3504.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: "neo" meaning "new" and "phutos" meaning "planted" or "growing." The image is therefore that of a plant freshly put in the ground. In the ancient Greek of the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), this word often renders the Hebrew "néta" (plant) or "shetil" (seedling), used to speak of young plants or young vines. The word has retained its botanical image in passing to the spiritual sense: a new convert is like a young plant that begins to grow.
G3504.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 3:6. The Apostle Paul uses it while giving instructions on the selection of overseers (deacons or elders) in the church. He warns that a recently converted man should not be elevated to this position, as his inexperience and nascent spiritual pride may cause him to fall under the judgment of the devil. In this context, "new convert" therefore designates a believer whose faith is still fresh, who has not had time to be tested and mature. It is a mark of pastoral wisdom: certain responsibilities require time and experience.
G3504.portee: This word reminds the reader that there are stages in Christian growth. A newcomer to the faith should not be entrusted immediately with the greatest burdens or responsibilities in the church. It also invites patience towards young converts and understanding that they need to be nurtured, taught, and humbly cared for until they take root. It is a call to ecclesiastical wisdom.

sens: Roman emperor of the 1st century
G3505.detail: Nero is the Roman emperor who reigned during the writing of Paul's second letter to Timothy. He is mentioned indirectly in this historical context.
G3505.origine: Nero (37-68 AD) is the fifth Roman emperor of the Julio-Claudian dynasty. His Latin name is Nero Claudius Drusus Germanicus. He reigned from 54 to 68 AD, a period marked by severe persecutions against Christians in Rome.
G3505.emploi: Nero appears in the subscription (historical title added to the text) of the second epistle to Timothy, which situates the letter historically at the time of his reign. It is under Nero's reign that Paul would have written this letter from Rome, shortly before his martyrdom. Nero is historically known for persecuting Christians, and accusations against him include the burning of Rome in 64 AD.
G3505.portee: The mention of Nero reminds the reader that Paul wrote to Timothy in a context of danger and persecution. It testifies to the faithfulness of Christ's disciples in the face of hostile authorities and emphasizes that the Gospel spread despite the opposition of earthly powers.

sens: To make a gesture with the head or hand to communicate without speaking
To give a signal or instruction to someone to do something
To silently command by a gesture
G3506.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the simple and natural gesture of nodding the head or making a hand sign to communicate. It is a discreet way to convey a message, often because one cannot speak or wants to remain discreet. At the Last Supper, Simon Peter "signaled to John" (John 13:24) to ask Jesus who the traitor is — he does not want to interrupt Jesus by asking the question himself.
2. The gesture can also express permission or an order. When Governor Felix "signaled" to Paul (Acts 24:10), it was to allow or command him to speak — Paul understands the gesture and begins his defense speech. The sign becomes here a silent command that replaces the word.
G3506.origine: The verb comes from a root that evokes the idea of movement of the head or body — as one "leans" or "turns" the head. In ancient Greek, the verb has retained this basic meaning: to make a gesture with the body, notably the head. The word family includes other compound verbs (with prefixes) that reinforce the idea: to signal towards, to signal down, to signal up and down, according to the direction of the gesture.
G3506.emploi: The verb appears twice in the New Testament, always in the aorist form (the simple past in Greek). In both cases, it involves an authority or a person communicating an order or intention through a simple gesture. At the table, Simon Peter uses this gesture to discreetly communicate with another disciple without disturbing Jesus. Before the tribunal, the governor uses it as an official gesture, equivalent to saying "You may speak." In both contexts, the gesture replaces the word and is sufficient to be understood.
G3506.portee: This word shows us how silent communication between men can be as clear as spoken words. It also reminds us that before God, we often only need to signal — an inner attitude, an inclination of the heart — rather than many words. It is a biblical detail that values simplicity and discretion in communication.

sens: A mass of visible water vapor in the sky
A concrete weather phenomenon that can obscure the sun
The miraculous cloud that guided Israel in the desert, a pillar of fire and smoke
A sign of the divine presence and the power of God
An image of the coming of Christ in His glory
A symbol of what temporarily hides or veils reality
G3507.detail:
1. It is primarily an ordinary cloud: Luke 12:54 refers to the clouds that everyone observes in the sky and that announce rain — something mundane and visible to all.
2. The cloud becomes a religious phenomenon when it accompanies manifestations of God: at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:5), a luminous cloud covers the disciples, and from this cloud comes the voice of the Father speaking about Jesus. It is a sign that God is present and speaking.
3. In the Old Testament, as referenced by Paul, the cloud was the physical guide of Israel: "baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea" (1 Corinthians 10:2), alluding to the cloud that protected the people in the desert.
4. The cloud is the throne or vehicle of the resurrected Christ: "coming on a cloud" (Luke 21:27) means that Jesus arrives in glory and power, as it was expected that God Himself would come. Revelation 1:7 confirms that "He comes with the clouds."
5. The cloud envelops and hides: the disciples at the Transfiguration "were terrified as they entered the cloud" (Luke 9:34), for it removes them from view.
6. It also evokes judgment and divine authority: in Revelation 14:14-16, a figure resembling the Son of Man is seated on a cloud with a sickle of gold, ready to judge the earth.
G3507.origine: The Greek word νεφέλη (nephelē) has the same root as νέφος (nephos, a large indefinite mass of vapor), but nephelē designates a unique and specific cloud, delimited. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it primarily translates עָנָן (anan), which carries a strong theological weight: the cloud is the visible expression of the presence of God. The cloud of the desert, the one that will cover Jesus at the Transfiguration, the one on which He will return — all of this draws its meaning from this biblical image of a God who manifests Himself by covering His people and revealing Himself in a veiled yet certain manner.
G3507.emploi: The word appears 21 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Revelation. The Synoptics use it for the Transfiguration (Matthew 17, Mark 9, Luke 9) and for the coming of the Son of Man (Matthew 24, Mark 13, Luke 21), always with the sense of majestic divine presence. In 1 Corinthians 10, Paul connects the cloud of the desert to the baptism of Israel, giving the word a sacramental significance. In Revelation (1, 10, 11, 14), the cloud surrounds celestial beings and angels, reinforcing the idea of a superhuman power and reality. The word thus always designates something specific and visible, linked to moments or states of divine manifestation.
G3507.portee: For the Christian, the cloud reminds us that God never manifests Himself randomly: at the Transfiguration, it veils and protects the disciples, then reassures them by attesting to the divinity of Jesus; at His coming, it will be the sign that the judgment and glory of Christ become visible to all. It teaches us that God makes His presence real while remaining beyond our full understanding — a reality that is both tangible and mysterious, calling for faith.

sens: tribe of Israel whose ancestor was Naphtali, son of Jacob
geographical region of Galilee in northern Israel
people or group identified by their tribal origin
G3508.detail:
1. Naphtali is the name of one of the twelve tribes of Israel, founded by Naphtali, son of Jacob and Bilhah. His descendants formed one of the main divisions of the chosen people. In Revelation 7:6, the tribe of Naphtali is listed among the twelve tribes whose elect are sealed by God.
2. The territory of Naphtali is a region of Galilee in northern Israel, bordering that of Zebulun. Matthew 4:13-15 places Capernaum, where Jesus settled, in this region and cites an ancient prophecy concerning "the people of Zebulun and Naphtali."
3. In Revelation, Naphtali designates the group of believers from this tribe who receive the divine seal on the day of final judgment.
G3508.origine: The name Naphtali comes from the Hebrew נַפְתָּלִי (Naphtali), which literally means "my struggles" or "my fight." It is the name given by Rachel to her son in Genesis 30:8, referring to the struggles and rivalries of her life. The Greek form Νεφθαλείμ is the standard transliteration of the Hebrew name in the New Testament.
G3508.emploi: Naphtali appears three times in the New Testament, always in geographical or eschatological contexts. Matthew mentions the region of Naphtali in Galilee to locate the ministry of Jesus, recalling a prophecy from the book of Isaiah that light would rise in these lands. Revelation lists the tribe of Naphtali among the twelve tribes whose faithful receive the divine seal, illustrating the continuity between the Israel of the Old Testament and the eschatological church. The name retains its identity and tribal heritage significance.
G3508.portee: Naphtali reminds the reader that Jesus fulfilled His ministry in the regions promised by the prophets of the Old Testament. The presence of Naphtali in Revelation 7 affirms that God never abandons His people: the historical tribes of Israel have their place in the divine plan of final redemption, not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit of the promise.

sens: A mass of clouds, a cloud as such
A dense, compact crowd, inseparable
G3509.detail: 1. The word νέφος primarily designates a cloud or a collection of clouds: a visible mass of water vapor floating in the atmosphere. This is the concrete and literal meaning that this word carries in common Greek. 2. Metaphorically, "cloud" evokes a crowd so compact and united that it forms a unified and almost solid whole — like a cloud that cannot be traversed. In Hebrews 12:1, Paul uses this word to speak of the witnesses that surround us: they form a "cloud of witnesses," a crowd so numerous and present that it surrounds us like an indivisible mass.
G3509.origine: The Greek word νέφος comes from an Indo-European root describing a cloudy or misty mass. In biblical Hebrew, it translates terms like עָב (a layer of clouds), עָנַן (a cloud), or שַׁחַק (the covered heavens). The image of the cloud, thick and enveloping, has naturally transposed into Greek to metaphorically describe a crowd or multitude.
G3509.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: Hebrews 12:1. Paul uses it in a highly poetic and metaphorical manner to exhort Christians. The "cloud of witnesses" refers to all those whose faith is recounted in the Old Testament and the previous episodes of the Epistle — believers who have died but whose example persists, enveloping the living like an invisible and motivating presence. This unique occurrence shows how the author chooses this precise word for its evocative power: not a simple "crowd," but a compact, intoxicating, almost palpable mass that urges the runner to persevere.
G3509.portee: This image of the "cloud of witnesses" reminds the Christian reader that he is never alone in his faith: generations of faithful believers, even deceased, surround and encourage him by their example. It transforms the solitude of the spiritual race into a communal act, inscribed in a long chain of testimony. This vision invites every Christian to live worthily, aware of this invisible presence that carries and watches over him.

sens: The organ of the human body that filters urine
That which symbolizes will, deep desires, and hidden intentions of the heart
G3510.detail:
1. The kidney is the well-known physiological organ. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word appears mainly in descriptions of worship and sacrifices, particularly to refer to the kidneys of animals offered to God (as in Exodus 29:13).
2. In biblical thought, the kidneys represent the seat of wills and intimate affections — the deepest and most secret parts of us. In Revelation 2:23, Jesus says, "I search the kidneys and the hearts": He scrutinizes not only what we feel (the heart) but also what we truly want, our hidden desires, our secret motivations. This is a call to total authenticity before God.
G3510.origine: The Greek word nephros corresponds to the Hebrew כִּלְיָה (kil'yâh), which designates the anatomical kidney. In the Hebrew Bible, this physiological word has taken on a symbolic value: the Hebrews saw in the kidneys the seat of deep emotions and intimate will, just as we speak of the "heart" for feelings. The Greeks retained this metaphorical image in translation.
G3510.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Revelation 2:23. Jesus speaks to the Church of Thyatira using language inherited from the Old Testament: "I search the kidneys and the hearts." This association of "kidneys-hearts" is classic in the Hebrew psalms (Psalm 7:9, 16:7, 26:2), where God scrutinizes the secrets of the faithful. In John, it is a statement of Christ's omniscience: He knows not only our visible acts but also our most hidden intentions.
G3510.portee: For the believer, this image invites sincere examination: no one can hide before God, who sees beyond appearances and words. It calls for seeking coherence between our true intentions and our outward life. It is an invitation to spiritual integrity and honest confession.

sens: A person responsible for maintaining and protecting a temple
An honorary title given to a city that houses an important sanctuary
G3511.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a guardian, someone who cares for and protects a temple (from the Greek "neo" = temple and "koros" = guardian). It is a concrete role: to watch over the sacred building, maintain it, protect it.
2. However, in Acts 19:35, when the town clerk of Ephesus says that his city is the "guardian" of the temple of Diana, he uses this title in an honorary sense: it is not a person, but an entire city that claims the prestige of being the seat of a world-renowned sanctuary. It is a political and religious honor.
G3511.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: "neo" (temple) and "koros" (guardian, one who takes care). The image is one of vigilant guarding. This title is attested in ancient inscriptions as an honorary distinction for cities that hosted prestigious sanctuaries.
G3511.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 19:35. In this scene of riot in Ephesus, the city clerk uses this title to calm the crowd and remind them how proud Ephesus is of its worship of Diana. It is an official and prestigious designation that cities competed to obtain from Roman authorities.
G3511.portee: This word shows us how ancient cities built their reputation and prestige around their temples. For Ephesus, the worship of Diana was not just a religious matter: it was a source of power, income, and identity. This sheds light on the context of the confrontation between the Gospel and local religions: the stakes were also social and economic.

sens: Belonging to youth, characteristic of young age
Proper to the desires and passions of young people
G3512.detail:
1. This word designates what is typical of youth, what marks young age. It is the adjective used to qualify traits, behaviors, or feelings natural to this stage of life.
2. More specifically, it applies to the passions and desires that boil within the young. Paul writes to Timothy: "Flee youthful passions" (2 Timothy 2:22), speaking of those carnal impulses and cravings that youth particularly inflames — not to condemn them, but so that Timothy can master and surpass them by seeking rather justice and faith.
G3512.origine: This word comes from the root meaning "young" and "new." It belongs to the family of Greek words designating youth (including "neos" = young, new). It is an adjective formed to describe everything related to this stage of life, with its freshness but also its inexperience and natural ardors.
G3512.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 2:22. Paul uses it to characterize the "passions" that Timothy, a young pastor, must combat. It is not merely a moral description, but a pastoral counsel: to recognize that certain desires are typically youthful, and that wisdom consists in mastering them by turning towards higher goods — justice, faith, charity, and peace.
G3512.portee: This word invites every young believer to recognize their condition: youth brings strengths and ardors, but also passions that can lead them away from God. The text does not invite to stifle youth, but to orient it. For a reader of all ages, it reminds us that maturing in faith means allowing our true desires to gradually transform — from carnal desires to justice, from agitation to peace.

sens: Particle of affirmation that reinforces a statement
Particle used to introduce an oath or vow
Expression of absolute certainty
G3513.detail:
1. This small Greek particle serves to affirm strongly what is said, like someone swearing on something sacred. In 1 Corinthians 15:31, Paul uses it to support his solemn declaration: "I face death every day, I affirm it" — he uses this particle to swear that his words are true, placing his affirmation under the seal of sincerity.
2. Originally, νή was linked to religious oaths: one swears "by" something sacred (in Greek, it is constructed with an accusative, meaning "by"). Paul thus swears "by the glory" of his brothers in Christ — which gives his phrase exceptional gravity.
3. Its literal effect is to say "as true as" or "as certain as" — it is an expression of absolute certainty. The context of the passage shows that Paul emphasizes the reality of the danger and suffering he constantly endures for the Gospel.
G3513.origine: The particle νή comes from an ancient root related to the idea of affirmation and oath. In Hebrew, the word חַי ("living") was commonly used in oaths ("as surely as God lives"), and in the Greek Bible, νή often represents it. It thus expresses the strength of a sworn affirmation, something serious and irrevocable.
G3513.emploi: This particle appears only once in the New Testament in the noted places: in 1 Corinthians 15:31. Paul uses it to swear, in technical terms, it introduces an oath, but with a particularity: he does not swear by the name of God, but by a spiritual reality (the glory of his brothers). It is a moment of remarkable intensity where the apostle insists on the constancy of his trials and his faithfulness despite daily danger. The rare use of this word precisely reinforces the emphasis he wants to place.
G3513.portee: This particle invites us to take Paul's affirmation seriously: every day, he risks his life for the Gospel. When an apostle uses such solemn and emphatic language, it is because he wants us to understand the reality of his sacrifice and conviction. This speaks to us of the true nature of Christian devotion: not a theory, but a daily and dangerous reality, embraced with assurance in faith.

sens: To twist and turn textile fibers to form a thread
In reference to flowers, to produce or shape their substance delicately
G3514.detail:
1. To spin means to transform raw fibers (wool, linen, hemp) into a continuous and strong thread by twisting and turning them together. It is a long and delicate manual work, traditionally done by women. Exodus describes the women of Israel spinning fibers for the garments of the tabernacle (Exodus 35:25).

2. Jesus uses this verb figuratively to evoke the delicate and laborious way living beings create themselves. In Matthew 6:28 and Luke 12:27, he says that the lilies of the field "neither toil nor spin," meaning they do not create their beauty by their own effort, but receive it from God. This image shows the contrast between human energy and divine creation: we weave our garment through our work, while creation springs forth from God's rest and power.
G3514.origine: The verb νήθω comes from a root that evokes the action of twisting and weaving. In ancient Greek, it translates the Hebrew טָוָה (to twist) and שָׁזַר in the causative sense (to interlace, to braid). This word belongs to the family of terms designating textile work, a fundamental area of ancient life, especially for women. Spinning was a daily task, so mundane that it became the very image of ordinary labor.
G3514.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, in Matthew 6:28 and Luke 12:27 — two parallel versions of the same teaching of Jesus. In these two passages, Jesus asks his disciples to "consider" the lilies of the field and to notice that they neither toil nor spin. The context is that of the Sermon on the Mount: Jesus teaches his disciples not to worry about their clothing, for God provides. The verb νήθω represents the quintessential type of human work — meticulous, repetitive, indispensable — that God renders unnecessary for natural creation, since He clothes it with beauty without its assistance.
G3514.portee: Jesus invites us to contemplate nature not as a soulless machine, but as the constant expression of divine care. If God causes the flowers to grow in their splendor without them making any effort, how much more will He care for His children? This word frees the believer from self-centered anxiety: our security does not rest on our eternal labor, but on the trust that God nourishes and clothes those He loves.

sens: To be in the state of a child, little child, baby
To remain naive or immature in judgment
To maintain a simple innocence in the face of evil
G3515.detail:
1. The verb literally designates being or acting like a little child, an infant. It is the natural state of one who cannot yet reason or defend themselves (1 Corinthians 14:20 says "do not be children in your thinking").
2. To be a child in judgment means lacking mental maturity: not knowing how to discern, to judge healthily, or remaining attached to simplistic and childish reasoning. Paul reproaches the Corinthians for this intellectual weakness.
3. Conversely, Paul exhorts to "be children" in the face of malice — that is, to maintain a simple, naive innocence, without complicity with evil. A child naturally ignores cunning and wickedness.
G3515.origine: The verb comes from the Greek adjective « népiος » (child, little child, infant). This root evokes the image of one who cannot yet speak (some see a link with the absence of speech). The word always carries this nuance of dependence and physical or moral immaturity.
G3515.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 14:20. Paul creates a contrast: the Corinthians must renounce childishness in their spiritual and intellectual judgment (regarding spiritual gifts and worship order), but maintain childlike innocence in the face of evil and cunning. It is a call to spiritual maturity combined with moral purity.
G3515.portee: This word reminds us that Christian maturity is not a cynical hardness: it requires cultivating two things together — clear discernment of spiritual realities, and the innocence of heart that refuses cunning and wickedness. For the Christian, growing up does not mean becoming malevolent, but becoming just and vigilant.

sens: Little child, young child
A person who lacks maturity or knowledge
A new believer or spiritually immature
G3516.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the small child, one who has just been born or is still in the womb. Jesus cites the praises that come "from the mouth of children" (Matthew 21:16), referring to very young children.
2. More broadly, it describes one who lacks judgment, discernment, or knowledge: the ignorant, the naive. Romans 2:20 speaks of the "teacher of the ignorant," referring to one who instructs people devoid of knowledge.
3. Figuratively, it designates the believer who remains spiritually childish, inexperienced, or fragile. Paul tells the Corinthians: "I could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to children in Christ" (1 Corinthians 3:1), meaning they have remained carnal rather than growing toward spiritual maturity. This is the opposite of one who is "perfect" or mature in faith.
G3516.origine: The Greek word νήπιος comes from a root that evokes the absence of speech or the inability to express oneself: literally "one who does not speak." It generally translates the Hebrew עוֹלֵל (olel), which designates the little child, particularly the infant. This etymology explains why the word also carries the meaning of one who knows nothing, who is deprived of knowledge or judgment.
G3516.emploi: This word appears about eleven times in the New Testament, particularly in Paul and in the Gospel of Luke. In the concrete sense, it designates young children, as in Matthew 21:16. In the figurative sense, Paul uses it abundantly to describe spiritual immaturity: the Corinthians remain "children in Christ" (1 Corinthians 3:1), and Hebrews 5:13 contrasts the child with the "perfect" believer. The contrast between childhood and maturity recurs often: 1 Corinthians 13:11 describes the transition from childhood to adulthood, while Ephesians 4:14 warns against remaining "children" tossed to and fro by every wind of doctrine. Galatians 4:1-3 also speaks of the minor heir, who remains "a child" under guardianship.
G3516.portee: This word calls the reader to examine their own spiritual growth. Remaining "a child" in Christ means remaining weak, manipulable, unable to discern the truth. But it also reminds us that Jesus receives and values children, and that the innocent simplicity of a little child can be a model of trust in God. The biblical call is to grow without ever losing that childlike trust.

sens: Christian from Rome greeted by the Apostle Paul
G3517.detail: Nereus is a man (or possibly a woman, as the name can bear both genders) who lived in Rome during the time of the Apostle Paul. Paul greets him by name in his letter to the Romans, which shows that Nereus is part of the believers in the Christian community of Rome and is personally known to the apostle or at least esteemed (Romans 16:15).
G3517.origine: Outside the New Testament, this name Nereus comes from Greek mythology: he was a sea god, son of Pontos (the Sea itself) and father of the Nereids, the goddesses of the sea. Paul uses it here simply as the name of a real person living in Rome, without reference to this pagan mythology.
G3517.emploi: Nereus appears only once in the Bible: in Romans 16:15. Paul, writing from Corinth to the Christians in Rome, lists the names of brothers and sisters to greet them personally. Nereus is mentioned alongside Philologus, Julia, his sister, and Olympas, suggesting that this is a group of believers connected by friendship or perhaps family. This enumeration shows that, even if he did not know Rome personally, Paul had reliable information about the faithful who composed it.
G3517.portee: This simple verse reminds us that every Christian, even the most discreet, is known and counted by the Lord and can be worthy of mention in Scripture. Nereus also shows us that the early Church was composed of very ordinary people, identified by a name, integrated into bonds of family or friendship.

sens: Ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy of Luke
G3518.detail: Neri is a man who appears in the genealogy of Jesus reported by Luke in chapter 3. He is the father of Salathiel and the son of Joanan. This genealogy traces the line of descendants from Adam to Jesus, and Neri occupies a place in this genealogical chain that establishes the legal and spiritual origins of the Messiah.
G3518.origine: The name Neri comes from the Hebrew Neriya (נֵרִיָּה), which literally means "light of the Lord" or "my lamp is the Lord." It is a name borne in the post-exilic period, after the return of the Jews from Babylon. The name reflects the faith of the parents in divine guidance.
G3518.emploi: Neri appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:27, in the genealogy of Jesus. This unique occurrence shows that Luke includes Neri among the ancestors of Jesus after the Babylonian exile. This detail reminds us that Jesus descends from a complete human lineage, rooted in the history of Israel.

sens: A small-sized island
A land surrounded by water of reduced dimensions
G3519.detail:
1. A small island is a land surrounded by water of modest size, unlike a large island. The Greek word is formed with a diminutive, emphasizing the reduced nature of this land. In Acts 27:16, Paul and his companions pass under Clauda, a small island near Crete, during the storm that carries them to Rome.
2. The term concretely designates an insular geographical formation: a land completely surrounded by water, but of limited extent, small enough to be noticed as distinct from larger lands or archipelagos.
G3519.origine: The word comes from the Greek νῆσος (nêsos, "island"), to which a diminutive suffix (-ιον) has been added. This suffix expresses smallness or a diminished form of the main concept. The root itself simply evokes a land isolated by water, an ancient notion in Greek since Homer and Herodotus.
G3519.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:16. Paul, a prisoner on his way to Rome, is caught in a storm. Passing near Clauda (a small island in the Mediterranean, south of Crete), the ship's crew finds a moment to secure the lifeboat. The context shows that even a small island can provide valuable help to distressed sailors by creating a slightly calmer water area.
G3519.portee: This mention reminds us how God provides for the needs of His children, even in the most difficult circumstances. The small island of Clauda becomes a refuge in the storm, illustrating that nothing is too small or insignificant to serve God's plans for His apostles.

sens: Land surrounded by water on all sides
Place of isolation or refuge
Figuratively: fragile space that disappears
G3520.detail:
1. An island is a land completely surrounded by the sea. This is the concrete meaning of the word, which we find when Paul shipwrecks and arrives at Malta: "we recognized that the island was called Malta" (Acts 28:1). The islands of the Mediterranean mark the journeys of the apostles and serve as stopping points or stages in their missionary itinerary.
2. An island can also evoke isolation or refuge. John writes Revelation on the island of Patmos (Revelation 1:9), separated from the rest of the world, in a solitude that fosters prophetic vision. It is a space apart, distinct from the continent.
3. In apocalyptic vision, islands become an image of fragility: "all the islands fled away" (Revelation 6:14) and "there were no more islands" (Revelation 16:20) symbolize a world in dissolution at the end of times, where even solid lands disappear.
G3520.origine: The Greek word νῆσος (nēsos) is an ancient Indo-European term designating a mass of land surrounded by water. It already appears in ancient Greek epic. In Hebrew, the corresponding word is אִי (î), which literally means "shore" or "coast" before designating the island itself. This word reflects the geographical reality of the Mediterranean, dotted with islands, and of ancient Greece, an insular world par excellence.
G3520.emploi: The word νῆσος appears 9 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Acts and Revelation. In Acts, it designates real places: Cyprus (Acts 13:6), Malta (Acts 28:1), and other islands of the Mediterranean that Paul traverses on his journey to Rome. These references are very concrete and geographical — they mark the stages of a missionary journey. In Revelation, the word takes on an apocalyptic meaning: the island of Patmos becomes the place of revelation, and the islands become cosmic images of what must disappear at the final judgment (Revelation 6:14, 16:20). The context shifts the word from the real to the symbolic.
G3520.portee: For the reader of the early Church, the island reminds us how God extends the testimony of the Gospel to the ends of the known world, even to isolated lands. It also symbolizes, by extension, refuge and perseverance in separation: John, isolated on Patmos, receives the vision that will guide the Church until the end of times. In apocalyptic terms, the fleeing island invites us not to anchor our hope in this transient world.

sens: voluntary abstention from food to dedicate oneself to prayer or penance
involuntary deprivation of food
period of time marked by abstinence from food
G3521.detail:
1. Fasting is primarily a voluntary act of spiritual discipline: one abstains from eating to turn more towards God and prayer. Jesus teaches that certain spiritual challenges can only be overcome through fasting and prayer together (Matthew 17:21). The early Church fasted when praying for important decisions, such as the selection of elders (Acts 14:23). The prophetess Anna spent her life as a widow in the temple, serving God "night and day in fasting and prayer" (Luke 2:37), showing how fasting expresses total devotion.
2. Fasting can also be a suffering endured, not chosen: Paul lists the deprivations he has endured — involuntary fasting — alongside beatings and imprisonments (2 Corinthians 11:27). This is a forced hunger, not a spiritual discipline.
3. The word also designates the holy period marked by mandatory abstinence, such as the Day of Atonement among the Jews (Acts 27:9).
G3521.origine: The Greek word νηστεία comes from the verb νηστεύω (to fast), formed from the root νη- (not) and σίτος (food): literally "not eating." It translates the Hebrew צוֹם (tsom), which has the same structure: deprivation of food. In Greek, the word also appears in ἀσιτία (another word for fasting), but νηστεία is the dominant term in the New Testament to designate fasting as a religious practice.
G3521.emploi: The word νηστεία appears 8 times in the New Testament. Its usage shows two complementary dimensions. First, voluntary fasting related to prayer: Matthew and Mark mention it in the context of spiritual power against demons; Luke and Acts show it as a practice of pious Christians (Anna, the elders of the Church). Secondly, involuntary fasting: Paul lists it among his apostolic sufferings (2 Corinthians). Acts 27:9 shows that the term can also designate a holy calendar period (the Day of Atonement, when fasting was imposed by the Law). Finally, 1 Corinthians 7:5 uses the word in a metaphorical sense: "devote" to prayer means temporarily dedicating oneself to prayer by abstaining from other activities.
G3521.portee: Biblical fasting is never an end in itself, but a means of turning towards God. Jesus' teaching shows that it accompanies prayer to confront spiritual challenges. This invites the Christian to view fasting not as superstition or empty asceticism, but as a humble discipline that strengthens intercession. The example of Anna and the elders of the Church reminds us that it is an ancient and serious practice, not a modern whim.

sens: To abstain from food for a determined period
To practice this abstinence as an expression of piety or religious mourning
To voluntarily deprive oneself through spiritual discipline or in anticipation of divine intervention
G3522.detail:
1. To fast means to stop eating for a certain time. Jesus himself fasted for forty days in the desert (Matthew 4:2). It is a concrete physical act: the body deprives itself of food.

2. In the Bible, fasting also means expressing respect towards God or sorrow through this gesture. The disciples of John and the Pharisees fasted as a regular religious practice (Mark 2:18). It is a way to show that something important is happening on a spiritual level.

3. Fasting can also be a voluntary, free, and sincere personal act, detached from mere habit or the desire to appear pious. Jesus teaches that true fasting should not be ostentatious (Matthew 6:17-18): you should anoint your head and wash your face so that no one knows you are fasting, except your Father who sees in secret. It is a discipline of the heart, not a spectacle.
G3522.origine: The Greek word comes from νῆστις (nèstis), which literally means 'one who has not eaten' or 'who is fasting'. It thus expresses the state of one who abstains from food. The Hebrew word צוּם (tsoum), which this Greek verb translates in the Greek Old Testament, has the same root and the same concrete meaning: to abstain from eating as an act of mourning or supplication before God.
G3522.emploi: This verb appears 16 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels and Acts. It primarily describes the Jewish religious practice known to the disciples of John the Baptist and the Pharisees (Mark 2:18), who regularly fasted. Jesus himself fasts in the desert (Matthew 4:2) and teaches how to fast correctly — in secret, without seeking the glory of men (Matthew 6:16-18). After the resurrection, Jesus indicates that his disciples will fast 'on that day' (Mark 2:20), making fasting a future practice of the Church. In Acts, Christians fast before making important decisions: Paul and Barnabas fast before being sent on a mission (Acts 13:2-3). The word always expresses a voluntary approach, never a forced deprivation.
G3522.portee: For the Christian today, fasting reminds us that the body and its needs do not dominate spiritual life. It is a means of clarifying one's mind, showing God that certain things matter more than comfort. Fasting, when sincere and secret, becomes an act of humility and dependence on God. Jesus does not compel anyone to fast, but he validates this practice as legitimate for those who choose it with a pure heart.

sens: The state of one who has not eaten for a certain time
Voluntary abstention from food for spiritual or religious reasons
G3523.detail:
1. Fasting first simply describes the physical state: not having eaten anything. In the two passages of the Gospel, Jesus is concerned that the crowd might go away 'hungry' (Matthew 15:32 and Mark 8:3), meaning without having eaten for three days. It is an urgent bodily need: people will lack strength on the way.
2. More broadly, fasting can also be a voluntary practice, an intentional abstention from food. Although this figurative sense is not developed in these two verses, it is the same notion of not eating, but chosen for a religious or spiritual reason rather than imposed by circumstances.
G3523.origine: The Greek word νῆστις comes from a negative root (νη-) combined with a word meaning 'to eat'. Its etymology literally 'one who does not eat' makes it an adjective describing the state of one who abstains from food. It is a poetic term in classical Greek, later adopted in the New Testament to express this physical and spiritual condition.
G3523.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Gospels, both in Matthew and Mark, in parallel passages where Jesus multiplies the loaves. Jesus refuses to let a crowd that has followed him for three days go without eating. In these two contexts, fasting is the state of physical exhaustion, a situation where people lack vital strength. Jesus shows his compassion by providing for their bodily need.
G3523.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus does not disregard our physical needs. Feeding the hungry is an act of concrete compassion and love. Fasting, the state of hunger and weakness, becomes an opportunity to see how Jesus cares for the whole person, body and soul.

sens: One who is not moved or agitated, who masters their emotions
One who practices restraint and temperance in conduct
One who has good judgment and acts wisely
G3524.detail:
1. To be sober is primarily to maintain emotional balance and not be dominated by passions. It is a self-control that shows maturity. In 1 Timothy 3:2, an overseer is asked to be sober in order to properly lead the assembly of believers.
2. This word also describes a temperate person, who does not live in excess. In Titus 2:2, older men must be sober, meaning they should avoid extremes and show a balanced and orderly life.
3. Sobriety is related to the ability to judge well and act with discernment. In 1 Timothy 3:11, women must be sober to be trustworthy in the church.
G3524.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that evokes the idea of not being intoxicated or troubled. Originally, in classical Greek, it referred to a drink that was not mixed with wine. This material sense has gradually extended to a moral quality: one who is sober in wine becomes one who is sober in mind and judgment. The metaphor goes from the body to the heart.
G3524.emploi: This word appears three times in the New Testament, all in the pastoral epistles (1 Timothy and Titus). Paul requests it for church leaders: the overseer must be sober (1 Timothy 3:2), women in the church must be sober (1 Timothy 3:11), and older men must serve as models of sobriety (Titus 2:2). In all cases, it is a moral virtue expected of mature believers who have responsibilities or influence. Sobriety appears as an indispensable trait of Christian leadership.
G3524.portee: Sobriety is a virtue that every responsible Christian must cultivate. It reminds us that spiritual maturity involves self-control and balance in all things. For a church leader, this quality strengthens the trust of believers and the moral authority of service. It is also an invitation not to be dominated by emotions or passions, but to maintain clear judgment and orderly conduct.

sens: Not to be drunk, to abstain from wine
To be vigilant, attentive, clear-minded
To be self-controlled, to keep one's mind in check
To live with prudence and moral discernment
G3525.detail:
1. To be sober primarily means not to be drunk: it is to abstain from drinking wine excessively or losing one's reason through alcohol. It is a physical state of clarity.
2. However, the word is also used figuratively: to be sober means to be vigilant and mentally awake, like someone who is not sleeping and keeps their eyes open. In 1 Thessalonians 5:6, Paul says, "let us be alert and sober"; the two go together, it is to keep one's mind alert.
3. To be sober also means to master one's thoughts and emotions, to remain calm and composed. In 1 Peter 5:8, one must "be sober" in the face of the devil who "prowls around like a roaring lion": it is not to panic, not to lose one's mind.
4. More broadly, it is to live with prudence, discernment, and moral wisdom. In 1 Peter 1:13, Paul connects this to hope: "gird up the loins of your mind, be sober" — it is to bring order to one's thoughts and choices.
G3525.origine: The Greek verb νήφω comes from a root that evokes the physical state of clarity (the opposite of being dazed by alcohol). In Hebrew from the Old Testament, it could be related to the idea of watchfulness and vigilance. The word belongs to a Greek family that also includes « ἐκνήφω » (to wake up, to come to one's senses): all these words share the image of the mind being clear, lucid, "awake." It is a common word in the morality of the early Christians.
G3525.emploi: The verb "to be sober" appears six times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles of Paul and Peter. It is used only in moral appeals addressed to Christians: never to describe an event, but always as a command or exhortation. In 1 Thessalonians, Paul contrasts it with sleep: to be sober is to remain spiritually awake. In 1 Peter, the word appears three times (1:13, 4:7, 5:8) in the context of the last days and spiritual warfare: it is the vigilance of the disciple in the face of trials and danger. In 2 Timothy 4:5, Paul urges Timothy to be sober "in all things" — it is a general virtue of the servant of God. The context is always eschatological or pastoral: it is about remaining clear-minded while awaiting the return of Christ or in the face of temptations.
G3525.portee: For the Christian, to be sober is not just to abstain from alcohol — it is to keep one's mind clear and judgment intact in the face of the seductions of the world, fears, and temptations. It is a constant spiritual vigilance: to remain awake to the presence of God and the stakes of one's faith. In a world that seeks to lull and daze, this virtue reminds that the disciple of Jesus must maintain all their lucidity to discern His will and live faithfully while awaiting His return.

sens: nickname of a man named Simeon
G3526.detail: Niger is a nickname given to Simeon, one of the prophets and teachers of the Church in Antioch during apostolic times. It is a personal sobriquet, likely related to the physical appearance or origin of this man.
G3526.origine: Niger is the Latin word meaning "black." It is a Latin sobriquet used as a nickname, suggesting that Simeon was known by this name in the Greek-speaking and Latin-speaking community of Antioch. This type of nickname was common in antiquity to distinguish people with the same name or to describe a characteristic trait.
G3526.emploi: Niger appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 13:1, where it designates Simeon, one of the five prophets and teachers mentioned in the Church of Antioch. Simeon called Niger is listed alongside Barnabas, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen, and Saul (who would become the apostle Paul). This context indicates that Niger was a respected figure endowed with the prophetic gift in the young Church, despite his nickname possibly alluding to his origins or appearance.

sens: Man chosen by the assembly in Jerusalem to serve the distribution of aid to widows
G3527.detail: Nicanor is one of the seven men elected by the disciples in Jerusalem during the early days of the Church to assist the apostles in practical service: serving at tables, organizing food and aid for the widows of the community (Acts 6:5). His Greek name suggests that he was probably a Hellenistic Jew, meaning a Jew who spoke Greek, capable of communicating with the Greek-speaking widows of the Church.
G3527.origine: Nicanor is a Greek name composed of « nicé » (victory) and « andros » (man): literally "the one who is a victorious man." It was a common name in the Greek world. No Hebrew etymology explains its form.
G3527.emploi: Nicanor is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Acts 6:5, at the time when the apostles ask the assembly to elect seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, to take charge of the service of tables and distributions of aid. Nicanor is among the seven chosen, alongside Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas. This list shows that trustworthy men were selected for a task of material management and charity.
G3527.portee: The choice of Nicanor illustrates the early Church's concern to reconcile spiritual life and concrete assistance: the apostles could not do everything alone, and entrusting practical tasks to other competent and faithful men was an act of wisdom and faith. His Greek name reminds us that the Gospel brought together Jews of all origins, whether Greek-speaking or not.

sens: To overcome an opponent by force or authority
To achieve victory, to triumph
To dominate or master something hostile
To persevere in the face of opposition or evil
To obtain the ultimate victory (spiritual sense)
G3528.detail: 1. To overcome an opponent by force or authority: this is the most concrete meaning, that of a military victory or a fight. When someone stronger than another "subdues" them (Luke 11:22), they master them and strip them of their weapons. 2. To achieve victory, to triumph: the term denotes the result of a fight or trial. The one who "has triumphed" over the world (1 John 5:5) comes out victorious, without being defeated. 3. To dominate or master something hostile: one can conquer not only people but also evil forces. Young men "have conquered the evil one" (1 John 2:13), which means they have neutralized or overcome him. 4. To persevere in the face of opposition or evil: "overcome evil with good" (Romans 12:21) means not to be crushed by evil, but to surpass it in virtue. 5. To obtain the ultimate victory: in Revelation, "the one who conquers" (Revelation 2:26) will receive future promises, which evokes an eschatological victory, the final victory of Christ and His saints.
G3528.origine: The word comes from the Greek root nikē, which means "victory" or "success." This root appears in many compound words and fundamentally denotes the idea of surpassing, of winning. In the Septuagint (the Greek version of the Old Testament), this verb translates Hebrew words like zakah ("to be just, to be right") and hamad ("to desire, to covet"), showing how biblical Greek can give the word conquer a broader meaning than mere military victory.
G3528.emploi: The verb is used 24 times, mainly in the New Testament, particularly in Revelation and the epistles of John. Jesus "will conquer" or "has conquered" the world and its forces (John 16:33; Revelation 5:5; 17:14). Believers are also called to "conquer": John invites them to conquer the evil one (1 John 2:13-14), the world (1 John 5:4-5), evil (Romans 12:21). In Revelation, the promises addressed to those who "conquer" recur like a refrain (Revelation 2:7, 11, 17, 26; 3:5, 12, 21; 21:7). The term also denotes the victory of the Beast over the saints (Revelation 11:7; 13:7), reminding us that conquering is not automatic, but a challenge of spiritual warfare.
G3528.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that the Christian life is a spiritual battle, not passivity. Jesus has already conquered the world (John 16:33), and the Christian is called to share in this victory by remaining faithful, refusing evil, and persevering to the end. The promises made to the one who conquers (authority, crowns, eternal life) show that victory is not illusory, but real and rewarded. It is a word of hope and encouragement for the believer in the face of trials and opposition.

sens: Success achieved in a battle or struggle
Triumph over an opponent or obstacle
The act of overcoming what opposes
Spiritual domination acquired through faith
G3529.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes the success achieved in a military battle or physical confrontation: the one who wins the battle has the victory. 2. More broadly, it is the triumph over any opponent or obstacle that resists: overcoming an illness, surmounting a difficulty. 3. In figurative and spiritual usage, victory is the act of dominating, prevailing over what opposes us. 4. In 1 John 5:4, Paul uses "victory" to denote the triumph of faith: the one born of God "overcomes the world," and "our faith" is this victory that enables us to overcome the opposition of the world hostile to God.
G3529.origine: The Greek word nikē comes from a root meaning "to conquer" or "to overcome." It is related to the verb nikaō (to conquer). In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often translates the term netzah, which evokes the splendor and victory of God. The word evokes the concrete image of a warrior who wins victory on the battlefield, before extending to all areas where one triumphs over resistance.
G3529.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament in 1 John 5:4. In this passage, John speaks of the victory that the believer born of God achieves over the world (the system of values, the forces, and the temptations of the world that oppose God). He does not use the word for a military or political victory, but for spiritual domination: faith in Jesus Christ is the power that allows us to triumph over the obstacles and pressures of the world. This context shows that the victory he speaks of is a current reality for the believer, not a distant promise.
G3529.portee: This word enriches the reader's faith by showing that the believer is not passive in the face of the world: he possesses within him, through his birth from God and his faith, a true victory. It is neither military nor temporal, but spiritual — an inner domination over temptations, fears, and values contrary to the Gospel. Knowing that our faith is victory encourages us to stand firm in the face of the pressures of the world and to see our life as believers as a triumph, not a defeat.

sens: A Jewish religious leader during the time of Jesus
A Pharisee curious to understand Jesus
A man seeking the truth in secret
A disciple who acknowledges Jesus after His resurrection
G3530.detail:
1. Nicodemus is a Pharisee (a member of the Jewish religious elite) and a ruler of the Jews — that is, an important figure in the council or Sanhedrin. John 3:1 presents him this way from the outset to show that one cannot assume that a man of such authority and religious knowledge automatically understands the Kingdom of God.
2. He comes to question Jesus by night (John 3:2 implicit in 3:1-4), which signals both his personal curiosity and perhaps his fear of being seen with Jesus by his peers. His dialogue with Jesus about the new birth (John 3:4, 9) shows a man who initially only grasps the carnal meaning of Jesus' words: "How can a man be born when he is old?"
3. He is also a man of moral courage who, in the Sanhedrin, defends Jesus by reminding his colleagues that the Law does not condemn anyone without hearing him (John 7:50).
4. Finally, after the crucifixion, Nicodemus performs an extraordinary act of devotion: he comes with about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes to bury the body of Jesus (John 19:39), showing that he has converted and now openly confesses his faith in the resurrected one.
G3530.origine: The Greek name Νικόδημος (Nikodēmos) literally means "victory of the people" — it comes from niké (victory) and démos (people). It is a common name in the Greco-Roman world. John is the only one to mention this character, and he identifies him exclusively by his social and religious role in Jerusalem.
G3530.emploi: Nicodemus appears five times in the Gospel of John, always in connection with the person and teaching of Jesus. First, he comes to Jesus "by night" (John 3:1-9) for a conversation about spiritual regeneration — this passage has given rise to the theological concept of "new birth." Then, in John 7:50, while the Sanhedrin wants to arrest Jesus, Nicodemus timidly intervenes to defend the right to a fair trial. Finally, after the crucifixion, Nicodemus appears alongside Joseph of Arimathea to honor the body of Jesus (John 19:39). His journey illustrates a gradual transformation: from cautious curiosity to public faith.
G3530.portee: Nicodemus embodies the path of a man for whom knowledge and religious status are not enough to save: he needs a personal encounter with Jesus and a spiritual new birth. His story encourages the reader: one is never too anchored in one's certainties or too fearful to come to the light of Jesus. He is also a model of discreet growth in faith — he does not become a disciple "openly" until later, but his final devotion is complete and courageous.

sens: group of false believers in the first century
followers of a heretical doctrine opposed by Jesus
G3531.detail: 1. The Nicolaitans are a group of false professing Christians who infiltrated the churches of Ephesus and Pergamum in the first century. Jesus, speaking to the church in Ephesus in Revelation, praises the believers: "You hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate" (Revelation 2:6). 2. They propagate a false doctrine, a teaching that Jesus vehemently disapproves of. In Pergamum, He reproaches some Christians for being "similarly attached to the doctrine of the Nicolaitans" (Revelation 2:15). Although the Bible does not specify the details of this doctrine, early Christians who speak of it describe it as encouraging idolatry and immorality.
G3531.origine: The name likely comes from Nicholas, a Greek name meaning "victor of the people." Some early Christians associated this movement with a Nicholas mentioned in Acts 6:5 as one of the seven deacons chosen to serve, but without absolute certainty. The Greek suffix -ites indicates belonging to a group or movement.
G3531.emploi: The Nicolaitans appear only in Revelation, in two verses of chapter 2. The risen Jesus addresses reproaches to two churches: He commends Ephesus for hating their works, while He blames Pergamum for tolerating this doctrine within the community. This opposition shows that Jesus takes the doctrinal and moral integrity of His churches very seriously. The Nicolaitan movement represents one of the major internal threats to the nascent churches of the first century.
G3531.portee: This passage warns the church to remain vigilant against false teachings that arise from within and claim to offer spiritual freedom that is, in reality, carnal. Jesus teaches us that true faithfulness consists in discerning and rejecting doctrines that compromise holiness, even if they seduce with their promises. It is a timeless call to doctrinal clarity and moral integrity within the Christian community.

sens: Man chosen as a deacon in Jerusalem
Proselyte from Antioch
G3532.detail: Nicholas is one of the seven men elected by the church in Jerusalem to serve the widows and distribute material aid, alongside Stephen and Philip (Acts 6:5). He is designated as a "proselyte from Antioch," meaning a non-Jew who converted to Judaism before joining the Christian community.
G3532.origine: The name nicolaos (Νικόλαος) comes from ancient Greek: nikê, "victory," and laos, "people." It literally means "one who conquers the people" or "victory over the people." It is a Greek name borne by several figures in antiquity.
G3532.emploi: Nicholas appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 6:5, where he is counted among the seven deacons appointed to assist the apostles in serving the needy. His Antiochian origin and status as a proselyte highlight the openness of the early Church to converts from paganism.
G3532.portee: The choice of Nicholas illustrates how the early Church recognizes and integrates men of faith from diverse backgrounds. His role as a deacon reminds us that humble and concrete service to the poor is an honorable charge entrusted to those whom the Holy Spirit fills.

sens: City in Epirus, in northwestern Greece
G3533.detail: Nicopolis is a Greek city located in Epirus, a region of northwestern ancient Greece. Paul mentions that he intends to spend the winter there and asks Titus to join him there (Titus 3:12). It is in this city that the apostle plans to rest after his missionary work.
G3533.origine: The name "Nicopolis" literally means "city of victory" in Greek (nikè = victory, polis = city). It is located in Epirus, a historical region of ancient Greece, known for having several cities bearing this prestigious name.
G3533.emploi: Nicopolis appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in the letter to Titus. Paul refers to it as a winter residence he has chosen (Titus 3:12). The mention of this city reveals the movements of the apostle at the end of his missionary life and shows how he organized his periods of pastoral rest.

sens: The act of defeating an opponent or winning a battle
Triumph, final success after a struggle
Figuratively: the domination of justice or truth
The victory won by Christ over death and sin
G3534.detail:
1. Victory is the result of a struggle where one has defeated the opponent. It is military or sporting triumph, the favorable outcome of a battle. Jesus says that he will not break the bruised reed until he has made "justice triumph" (Matthew 12:20), meaning until justice completely prevails.
2. It is also the definitive success, the total accomplishment. Paul declares that "death has been swallowed up in victory" (1 Corinthians 15:54), meaning that the reign of death is entirely defeated and abolished.
3. The word expresses the power that triumphs over an obstacle or an enemy. When Paul asks, "O death, where is your victory?" (1 Corinthians 15:55), he questions death about the power it claimed, showing that it has lost it.
4. For Christians, victory is what God grants us through Jesus Christ: "Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ!" (1 Corinthians 15:57). It is the spiritual victory over sin and death, won by the resurrection of Christ and communicated to believers.
G3534.origine: The word νῖκος (nikos) is a late form of the ancient Greek νίκη (nikè), which means victory. It denotes the favorable outcome of a battle or rivalry. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew נֶצַח (netsakh), which also evokes definitive triumph. The meaning has enriched, moving from the military domain to the spiritual and moral domain, particularly in Paul’s writings to speak of Christ's victory over enemy powers.
G3534.emploi: The word appears four times in the Greek New Testament. Three occurrences are found in 1 Corinthians 15, where Paul discusses resurrection and the final victory over death: this is the key passage where victory becomes a central theological issue. One occurrence is found in Matthew 12:20, where Jesus cites a passage from the Septuagint regarding the Servant who makes justice triumph. Victory can denote an immediate triumph (making justice triumph in the gospel), but it especially carries an eschatological meaning in Paul: the ultimate victory over death and sin through the resurrection of Christ. It is a victory already real for the believer, but which will be fully realized at the end of times.
G3534.portee: This word reveals to the believer that their faith is not a passive resignation in the face of evil and death, but a participation in the victory that Jesus has already won. It calls the Christian to see beyond the present appearance: death no longer has the final word, and evil will not triumph. It is a word of encouragement and hope for those who are going through suffering or mourning, inviting them to rely on the power of the risen Christ.

sens: Inhabitant of the city of Nineveh, capital of Assyria
People known for their repentance in response to the preaching of the prophet Jonah
G3536.detail:
1. The Ninivites are the inhabitants of Nineveh, the great capital of the Assyrian empire, located in Mesopotamia (present-day Iraq). It is a pagan city, distant and foreign to the people of Israel.
2. In the Gospels, the Ninivites embody a striking example of repentance: "The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah" (Matthew 12:41). Although strangers to the faith of Israel, they responded to the prophet's call by repenting — a lesson that Jesus addresses to his Jewish contemporaries to challenge them.
G3536.origine: The word comes from the name Nineveh, the historical capital of Assyria, already mentioned in the Old Testament (Jonah 1:2; 3:2). The Greek suffix -ίτης means "inhabitant of" or "native of" — it is added to names of cities or peoples to form an adjective or a noun designating their inhabitants. It is a classical Greek formation that applies here to an eastern geographical name.
G3536.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in a context of comparison with Jesus and the generations of his time. Matthew (12:41) and Luke (11:32) report the same saying: Jesus asserts that the Ninivites will rise at judgment to condemn "this generation" (the Jews of his time) because they, strangers to the true God, repented at the preaching of an imperfect prophet, while his contemporaries refuse to repent despite his presence and signs. Luke (11:30) adds that Jonah was a sign for the Ninivites, as the Son of Man will be for this generation — an image of resurrection and judgment.
G3536.portee: The Ninivites challenge the Christian reader in two ways. First, their quick and complete repentance in response to the simple preaching of Jonah shows the power of the Word of God: no need for spectacular signs, the call to conversion is sufficient when the heart listens. Secondly, Jesus cites them to warn that the refusal to believe despite supreme evidence — his presence, his miracles, his resurrection — will be judged even more severely. It is an invitation not to harden one's heart, but to respond to God's call with the same promptness shown by those men of Nineveh.

sens: Shallow container designed to hold water
Utensil used for washing
G3537.detail:
1. The basin is an open, shallow, and wide container designed to hold water. It is a common household item used for various domestic tasks. In John 13:5, Jesus pours water into a basin to wash the feet of his disciples.
2. The basin serves a function of cleansing here: it contains the water necessary for the ritual washing of feet, a common practice of hospitality in the East. The act of Jesus kneeling to wash the feet of his disciples with the water from the basin is an act of humility and service toward those he loves.
G3537.origine: The word νιπτήρ (niptēr) comes from the Greek verb νίπτω (niptô), "to wash," particularly hands, feet, or face. It is a term regularly formed from this verb to designate the utensil used for washing. The word evokes the action of purifying oneself with water.
G3537.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 13:5, during the passage of the washing of the feet. In this context, the basin is not an ordinary object, but carries a spiritual significance: Jesus uses it to perform an act of humility toward his disciples, reversing the expected roles between the master and his servants. This gesture reveals the heart of Jesus' message about true service.
G3537.portee: The basin in John 13 reminds the Christian that true power is not in commanding, but in humble service. Jesus, the Lord, washes the feet of his disciples: this act invites every believer to serve others with the same selflessness and tenderness, without expecting recognition.

sens: clean a part of the body with water
wash oneself
wash hands according to a religious rite
wash feet as an act of service
G3538.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to clean a part of the body — face, hands, or feet — with water. It is a practical and daily act (Matthew 6:17, where Jesus tells the one fasting to "anoint your head and wash your face"), or an ordinary hygiene gesture.
2. In the reflexive form, the word means to clean oneself: the blind man "goes to the pool of Siloam and washes, and he receives his sight" (John 9:11), blending the physical gesture with its spiritual effect.
3. In a Jewish religious context, "washing" hands is part of a ritual practice: "the Pharisees do not eat unless they wash their hands thoroughly, according to the tradition of the elders" (Mark 7:3). It is an act of purification before a meal.
4. For Jesus, washing the feet of the disciples takes on a meaning of humble service and love: "he began to wash the disciples' feet and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded" (John 13:5). This gesture teaches that the master becomes a servant.
G3538.origine: The word νίπτω is a later form of the verb νίζω. It primarily translates the Hebrew רָחַץ (rachats), which means "to wash" or "to clean." In the Greek Bible, this verb is used for practical or ritual washings. The word belongs to the family of cleaning verbs, alongside λούω (to wash the whole body, to bathe) and πλύνω (to wash clothes).
G3538.emploi: The verb νίπτω appears 13 times in the New Testament. It is especially present in the Gospel of John, particularly in chapter 13 where Jesus washes the feet of his disciples — it is the central narrative that gives the gesture its spiritual depth: Jesus states, "If I do not wash you, you have no part with me" (John 13:8). The Gospels of Mark and Matthew use it for the ritual washings of the Pharisees (Mark 7:3, Matthew 15:2), and for ordinary hygiene (Matthew 6:17). John 9:7-11 recounts the miracle where the blind man washes at the pool of Siloam and regains his sight. The verb also denotes an act of charity towards widows (1 Timothy 5:10).
G3538.portee: This verb reveals two aspects of the Christian life. First, it shows that Jesus strips himself of his glory to serve his disciples: washing feet is not a prestigious act, but that of a slave, and Jesus performs it with love. Second, it calls the Christian to humility and mutual service — "Do you understand what I have done to you?" Jesus asks after this gesture (John 13:12). The physical washing becomes the image of an inner transformation.

sens: grasp with the mind the meaning of a word, teaching, or reality
perceive through reason or senses what is not immediately visible
reflect on something, think about it
have knowledge or awareness of something
G3539.detail:
1. To understand means to grasp with one's intelligence what one hears or reads. Jesus asks his disciples: "Are you also without understanding? Do you not understand?" (Mark 7:18), speaking of a spiritual truth they did not yet grasp. It is the mental act of receiving and welcoming a meaning.
