1. The word literally describes the act of dozing off, that is, closing one's eyes and gently slipping into sleep. This is what happens to the ten virgins in the parable who wait for the bridegroom: they "drowsed and fell asleep" (Matthew 25:5), exhausted from waiting.
2. Figuratively, to drowse means to be negligent or lack vigilance, like someone who sleeps when they should remain awake. It describes a state of inattention or letting go: one remains insensitive, detached, unresponsive.
3. More broadly, the word can express that something remains suspended, does not progress, or waits for its moment. The ruin of false teachers does not "drowse" (2 Peter 2:3): it does not sleep, it does not fall asleep—it is inexorably approaching.
G3573.origine: The verb comes from a root related to the idea of tilting or inclining the head (see νεύω, "to signal"). The image is that of the head drooping when one falls asleep. In ancient Hebrew, the corresponding word appears in the Psalms (121:4): the one who watches over Israel "neither slumbers nor sleeps." This verb captures the moment when vigilance weakens and consciousness fades.
G3573.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. First, Matthew 25:5 uses it literally to describe the sleep that surprises the virgins during their waiting. Then, 2 Peter 2:3 uses it figuratively and negatively: the ruin reserved for false teachers does not drowse, meaning it does not sleep, it does not fall asleep—the threat is constant and vigilant. These two usages show that the word oscillates between ordinary sleep and inertia or lack of action.
G3573.portee: This word reminds the believer of the danger of spiritual negligence. Like the virgins who drowse, one can lose their vigilance in faith, especially in the waiting for Christ. Conversely, it reassures: divine justice never drowses—it watches over the one who does evil, even if judgment is delayed. It is a call to remain awake and attentive.

sens: a period of twenty-four hours, a night and a consecutive day
G3574.detail: 1. The word designates a complete period of twenty-four hours, uniting night and day into a single duration. In 2 Corinthians 11:25, Paul recounts that after a shipwreck, he spent a day and a night adrift in the deep — that is, a full day, from evening to the next evening, without anyone's help.
G3574.origine: The Greek word combines two simple words: νύξ (nux), night, and ἡμέρα (hēméra), day. This combination creates an expression that designates the complete cycle of a twenty-four-hour period. The word is very rare — it appears only once in the New Testament — and shows how Greek can create compound words to express precise ideas.
G3574.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible: in 2 Corinthians 11:25, where Paul lists his sufferings in the service of the Gospel. He speaks of three shipwrecks, and after one of them, he spent a day and a night floating on the water. This extreme context — abandonment at sea — makes this duration even more terrible: no boat, no food, no visible help, just a full day and a night to survive. The word emphasizes the complete trial, without interruption.
G3574.portee: This passage reveals to the Christian the reality of the sufferings of the apostle Paul, which far exceed what is read in the book of Acts. His enumeration of trials — wounds, stoning, shipwrecks — shows that authentic service to Christ can demand a very heavy price and unimaginable dangers. It invites the reader to recognize Paul's faithfulness and, more broadly, that of all those who have given their lives without glory or recognition.

sens: A righteous man who lived before the flood and built an ark at God's command
Father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth, ancestor of all humanity after the flood
Biblical figure of faith and obedience in impossible situations
G3575.detail:
1. Noah is the man to whom God commanded to build an ark to escape the universal flood that was to destroy all humanity. Warned by God of this impending judgment, he obeyed in faith, even in the face of the general unbelief of his time. Matthew 24:37-38 shows that people would continue to live normally (eating, drinking, marrying) until the day Noah entered the ark and the flood destroyed them all.
2. Noah is the father of the three sons from whom all humanity descends after the flood: the genealogy in Luke 3:36 places him as the son of Lamech and father of Shem, thus establishing his place in the chain of human generations.
3. The epistle to the Hebrews 11:7 presents Noah as a model of faith: it was by faith that he believed the divine warning concerning invisible realities, that he built the ark despite the general doubt, and thus condemned the unbelieving world while becoming an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.
G3575.origine: The Hebrew name נֹחַ (Noah) probably means "rest" or "comfort." This name reflects hope: Lamech, his father, said when naming him that this child would bring relief from the toil and pain caused by the curse of sin. The New Testament uses the Greek name Νῶε, a transcription of the Hebrew term.
G3575.emploi: Noah appears 8 times in the New Testament, always in relation to the flood and divine judgment. Matthew 24 and Luke 17 mention him when Jesus teaches that the coming of the Son of Man will be sudden and unpredictable, comparable to the catastrophe of the flood: people will be engaged in their daily activities until the day judgment comes. Luke 3:36 simply includes him in the genealogy of Jesus. Hebrews 11:7 makes him a major example of biblical faith: although the flood was unthinkable in his time, Noah believed God's word and acted accordingly. The epistles of Peter also cite him as a witness of judgment by water. The New Testament never revisits the details of his life (the ark, the animals, the duration of the flood) but presents him as a type of the believer who believes in the invisible and obeys despite opposition.
G3575.portee: Noah teaches the Christian that true faith consists of believing God's word and obeying even when the entire context seems to contradict that word, and even when one stands alone in that obedience. His story reminds us that God judges and saves according to His justice, and that there is security only in trusting His revealed word. It also invites the reader not to be lulled into complacency by daily routine, but to remain vigilant in light of the reality of the coming judgment and divine intervention in history.

sens: Moving or acting without speed, with delay
Lacking promptness in understanding or receiving
Losing momentum, becoming slack
G3576.detail:
1. The word first evokes someone or something that moves slowly, without dynamism. In Hebrews 5:11, Paul tells his readers that they have "become slow to understand" — not stupid, but as if numb, lazy in their ability to grasp deep spiritual truths.
2. It also designates a moral or spiritual sluggishness: the one who is slow abandons their momentum, relaxes in their commitment. In Hebrews 6:12, the apostle warns against this laziness that would cause one to lose the fervor of faith and hope.
3. The image is that of an athlete or a walker who slows down and gives up, rather than one of natural incapacity.
G3576.origine: The Greek word νωθρός literally designates one who is numb, asleep, as if slowed in action. It comes from a root evoking sluggishness and drowsiness. In the Greek Old Testament (Proverbs 22:29), it translates a Hebrew word meaning darkness or lack of clarity — the idea of a mind that does not see clearly, that remains in a sort of fog.
G3576.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the epistle to the Hebrews, addressed to Christians who have received faith but are spiritually falling asleep. In Hebrews 5:11, it describes readers who are no longer progressing in understanding — they have closed their ears to deep teaching. In Hebrews 6:12, it warns against the risk of relaxing, of abandoning the race of faith. In both cases, the problem is not incapacity, but resignation: one has become slow because they have lost sight of their goal.
G3576.portee: This word calls every Christian to ask themselves if they are not falling asleep in their faith. It is not about guilt, but an invitation to maintain fervor, to progress in the knowledge of God, to remain vigilant. Spiritual sluggishness can affect even the most seasoned believer: that is why Hebrews exhorts us not to relax, but to imitate those who, with perseverance, inherit the promises.

sens: The rear part of the human body, from the shoulder to the waist
The attitude of one who flees or turns away, figuratively indicating submission or defeat
G3577.detail:
1. The back is the rear part of the human body, behind the thorax and abdomen. It is the area extending from the shoulders to the lower back. In Romans 11:10, the "continually bent back" is an image of the weight that burdens: it is the posture of one who bends under a load or shame.
2. Figuratively, having a bent back expresses submission, defeat, or lasting misfortune. When the back is bent, one no longer looks forward but downward: it is the biblical image of a soul crushed or turned away from the right direction. This figurative sense appears in Romans 11:10, where the curvature of the back signifies spiritual burden and distance from God.
G3577.origine: The word νῶτος comes from common Greek vocabulary to denote the rear part of the body. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it primarily translates כָּתֵף (shoulder) and עֹרֶף (nape), two words that also evoke postures of submission or refusal. The word has a simple somatic root: it first describes the physical body, then naturally extends to the figurative sense of attitude and fate.
G3577.emploi: The word νῶτος appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 11:10. Paul cites a passage from Psalm 69:23-24 to show that some Israelites have remained hardened against the Gospel. The image of the bent back symbolizes here the weight of divine judgment and spiritual blindness. It is not a medical description, but a prophetic image of burden and misfortune. The Pauline context emphasizes that this hardening is not final: it fits into a larger divine plan (mercy toward all, v. 32).
G3577.portee: This image of the bent back reminds the Christian reader that refusal of God leads to an overwhelming weight, a posture of defeat. It also invites both compassion toward the unbelievers and vigilance against the hardening of the heart. It is a call not to turn one's back on the grace offered in Christ.

sens: Place where one receives a guest, where one hosts them
Hospitality, welcoming the traveler
G3578.detail: 1. The lodging is primarily a physical place, a house or room where someone is received: it is the material location of welcome. In Acts 28:23, Paul arrives in Rome as a prisoner and is assigned a lodging, a fixed place where he can stay — it is in this lodging that many come to visit him to hear him speak about Jesus. 2. The word also refers to the act of welcoming, hospitality itself — this act of generosity that consists of opening one's home to a traveler. When Paul asks Philemon to prepare a lodging (Philemon 1:22), he speaks of both the physical place and the warm welcome he hopes to receive from the Christian community.
G3578.origine: The word comes from ξένος (xénos), which means "stranger" or "guest." It literally refers to the hospitality given to the stranger. In ancient Greek, xenia was a fundamental social virtue: welcoming the passing stranger was a moral duty, almost religious. This word expresses both the place and the human relationship it implies.
G3578.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, always with the meaning of lodging, a place of welcome. In Acts 28:23, it refers to the lodging assigned to Paul in Rome, where a long discussion with the Jews takes place. In Philemon 1:22, Paul asks for a lodging to be prepared for him, hoping to be released and able to visit Colossae. These two uses show the word in a context of travel and Christian hospitality, an important value in the early communities.
G3578.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds of the biblical importance of hospitality toward the stranger and the traveler. The early Church saw this welcome as an act of brotherly love and an expression of the Gospel. To welcome someone, to offer them lodging, is to recognize in them a brother or sister, and to testify to the new life in Christ.

sens: To receive someone as a guest, to offer hospitality
To welcome into one's home for a stay
To strike by strangeness, to surprise, to astonish
To appear bizarre or unusual
G3579.detail:
1. To welcome and host someone: to offer shelter and courteous reception. The verb denotes the concrete act of inviting someone into one’s home and providing for them. In Acts 10:23, Peter "lodges" his visitors after bringing them in; in Acts 21:16, the disciples bring Paul to Mnason, "with whom we were to lodge."
2. To be lodged, to be hosted by someone: to receive hospitality as a guest. In Acts 10:6 and 10:32, Simon Peter "is lodged" with Simon the tanner, indicating where to find him.
3. To surprise with something strange or unusual: to cause astonishment by presenting what is out of the ordinary. In Acts 17:20, the Athenians say to Paul: "You bring strange things to our ears" — the word here denotes the effect of surprise and disturbance.
4. To shock or seem bizarre due to its newness or contrary to expectations: to appear abnormal. In 1 Peter 4:4 and 4:12, Christians are surprised (even scandalized) by the new conduct of converts or by the sufferings of faith; the verb emphasizes the contrast between the usual way of life and the new one.
G3579.origine: The word comes from "xénos" (ξένος), which means "stranger" in the sense of both guest and foreigner. Greek hospitality toward the stranger gave rise to the verb "xenizō": to treat someone as a guest (to welcome them properly) or, by extension, to strike them with the unexpected (to treat them as something strange). The root evokes the idea of what comes from outside, from without, and can therefore surprise.
G3579.emploi: The verb appears ten times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Acts and the epistles of Peter and Paul. In Acts (about six uses), it denotes concrete hospitality: Peter lodges his visitors in Joppa, Paul is hosted in Malta and at Mnason's. The meaning enriches in Acts 17:20, where it expresses surprise at unusual teachings. In the epistles, the context changes: in Hebrews 13:2, the exhortation to "show hospitality to strangers" becomes a call to Christian hospitality toward unknown travelers. In 1 Peter 4:4 and 4:12, the passive verb "to be surprised" or "to be treated strangely" describes the astonishment of the pagans at the change in converts or the incomprehensible persecution of believers. The word thus navigates between the concrete action of welcoming and the inner attitude of astonishment.
G3579.portee: This word reminds Christians of the importance of hospitality toward others, especially toward the stranger, as a form of welcoming Christ himself (Hebrews 13:2). It also invites not to be surprised or discouraged when faith seems strange and unacceptable in the eyes of the world: the contrast between the new life in Christ and human expectations is normal and inevitable. It is an exhortation to faithfulness in strangeness.

sens: to welcome and house strangers, travelers
to receive kindly those who do not know us
to manifest Christian charity through welcoming
G3580.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the concrete action of welcoming a stranger or traveler into one's home, offering them a meal and shelter. This is a fundamental duty in Mediterranean and biblical culture: in 1 Timothy 5:10, Paul lists the good works of a godly widow, and among them is naturally "hospitality" — not as an abstract virtue, but as a visible practice towards those who arrive without resources or connections.
2. Beyond material lodging, the word encompasses all forms of welcoming reception: it is to do good to one who crosses the threshold, without judging or ignoring them. This welcome reflects a disposition of the heart — not to reject the unknown, but to treat them as a person worthy of respect.
3. For a Christian, practicing hospitality becomes a manifestation of charity and faith: to welcome the stranger is to serve Christ himself, as other passages in the New Testament remind us. It is love in action, made concrete by a simple gesture.
G3580.origine: The Greek word is composed of two roots: ξένος (xénos, "stranger, guest") and δέχομαι (déchomai, "to receive, to welcome"). The image is clear: it literally means "to receive the stranger." The term appears late in the Greek language in this form; it expresses a value that all ancient cultures esteemed, but which the Bible places at the heart of the life of God's people, particularly in the Old Testament where hospitality is an unwritten but sacred law.
G3580.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 5:10, where Paul lists the marks of a widow worthy of help in the Church. Hospitality is included among the essential "good works" — alongside caring for children, washing the feet of the saints, and helping the needy. Although the word is rare, the practice is omnipresent in the New Testament: hospitality is a distinguishing mark of the early Christian community, attributed to many figures such as Priscilla and Aquila or Gaius. Its absence from ordinary vocabulary may be due to the fact that Paul or the evangelists preferred more common terms or expressions, but this occurrence is sufficient to show its importance.
G3580.portee: For today's Christian, this word reminds us that faith is not evaluated by abstract feelings, but by tangible gestures. Welcoming the stranger, the traveler, or simply someone unfamiliar to us is to live the Gospel. This practice tests the authenticity of our charity and places us before the concrete responsibility we have towards one another — a lesson as urgent today as it was in Paul's time.

sens: One who comes from another country, another city
One who does not belong to a group, a community, a covenant
Unusual, surprising, out of the ordinary
One who arrives from outside, without ties to the place or community
One who is received, welcomed, or should be welcomed as a guest
G3581.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: a person from elsewhere, from a foreign country or city. In Athens, foreigners from other cities spent their time discussing the news (Acts 17:21). In Israel, at the time of Jesus' death, a potter's field was purchased to bury strangers, those who had no burial place in Judea (Matthew 27:7).
2. In a figurative sense, one who is excluded, without rights or belonging. The Ephesians, before their conversion, were "strangers to the covenants of promise" (Ephesians 2:12): they had no part in the covenant that God made with Israel. They were also "strangers and pilgrims on the earth" (Hebrews 11:13), an image of those who have no stable dwelling here.
3. What is unexpected, strange, out of the ordinary. A foreign teaching or doctrine surprises, shocks (Acts 17:18; Hebrews 13:9). A "strange" or unusual trial tests faith (1 Peter 4:12).
4. One who arrives from outside, without ties to the one who receives them. In the parable of Judgment, Jesus speaks of one who welcomes the stranger by giving them food and drink (Matthew 25:35, 43): this is an act of hospitality towards an unknown person.
5. In the practice of biblical hospitality, the stranger can also refer to one who is received, the guest (Romans 16:23 speaks of Gaius welcoming the apostle Paul) or the host who offers hospitality.
G3581.origine: The word ξένος (xénos) comes from an ancient Greek root evoking exchange and mutual welcome: in Greek culture, "xénia" (ξενία) means sacred hospitality, the bond created between a host and their guest. The corresponding Hebrew word נׇכְרִי (nokhrî) also means "stranger, one who is not from here." In ancient Greece, ξένος retained a less hostile connotation than simple: it is primarily one who is unknown, with whom one could create a bond of hospitality.
G3581.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the New Testament, mostly in Matthew, in Acts, and in the epistles. It primarily refers to a stranger in the literal sense, a foreigner from another region. But the apostle Paul, especially in Ephesians 2:12-19, plays on this word to describe the Gentiles who had no part in Israel's covenant: they were "strangers" to the promises, but the Gospel makes them citizens of God's people. Jesus uses "stranger" in his parable of the Last Judgment (Matthew 25:35-44) to teach that receiving an unknown person is to receive him. The epistle to the Hebrews (11:13) uses it to remind that the patriarchs knew themselves to be "strangers and pilgrims" far from their heavenly homeland. The word also takes on broader meanings: a foreign doctrine (Hebrews 13:9) surprises with its originality.
G3581.portee: This word broadens our vision of the Gospel. Jesus teaches that we must welcome the stranger, one who is not one of us, not out of social obligation but as we would welcome him ourselves. Paul reminds the Ephesians and the converted Gentiles that they were first "strangers" to the promises, but that the Gospel has "naturalized" them into the people of God, thus removing the wall of separation. Finally, Hebrews 11:13 tells us that true believers remain somewhat "strangers and pilgrims" on this earth: our true home is elsewhere, with God.

sens: a container made of wood or stone used to draw or pour water
an object of ritual purification in Jewish practices
G3582.detail:
1. A pitcher is a practical container, generally made of wood or stone, used to draw water or pour it. It is a common utensil, as ordinary as a glass or a carafe today. In Mark 7:4, Jesus mentions the washing of pitchers among other vessels.

2. Among the pious Jews of Jesus' time, this pitcher becomes a religiously significant object: it is ritually washed for purification before meals, according to the traditions of the elders. This is not a commandment of the Law of Moses, but a practice added by the Pharisees to demonstrate their piety. Mark 7:4 shows that Jesus criticizes this multiplication of human rules that distance one from the heart of the Law.
G3582.origine: The Greek word comes from the Latin "sextarius," a Roman measure of capacity (about a pint). The Greeks borrowed this term from the Romans and adapted it to their language. It originally refers to a measure of liquid, then by extension to the container that holds it. It is a pragmatic word, marked by the contact between cultures: the Roman measure becomes the Greek and Jewish vessel.
G3582.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Mark (7:4 and 7:8), and in a single context: that of the ritual purifications of the Pharisees. Mark mentions it when he lists the objects that traditional Jews wash before eating — pitchers, cups, bronze vessels. Jesus uses this list to show the absurdity of a piety that focuses on external purity (washing containers) instead of purifying the heart. The word is thus always linked to the evangelical critique of human traditions.
G3582.portee: This small pitcher teaches us a fundamental lesson: God does not care about meticulous scruples regarding human rules, even religious ones, if they are devoid of sincerity of heart. Jesus invites us to look beyond external gestures to true inner purity. For the Christian, it is a call not to transform faith into formal rituals forgotten of their meaning.

sens: To lose its moisture, to dry up (for a plant, a harvest)
To become dry, without water (for a liquid)
To atrophy, to weaken (for a body part)
Figuratively: to wither, to be cut off from its source of life
G3583.detail:
1. A plant that dries loses all its moisture and dies: this is what happens to the seed that falls on rocky ground without deep roots (Matthew 13:6), or to the fig tree cursed by Jesus that completely dries up overnight (Mark 11:21). The image shows the absence of water, thus the absence of life.
2. A liquid that dries disappears: this is the case of the sea that dries up at the end of times (Revelation 16:12). A few hours are enough to drain what was abundant.
3. A body part that dries stiffens and atrophies: the possessed boy becomes completely stiff in his movements (Mark 9:18), as if the natural moisture and flexibility of his body had withdrawn. This is also what happens to a withered hand (Mark 3:1), paralyzed and unusable.
4. In the image of the vine in John, the branch that does not remain in Jesus dries up and is thrown into the fire (John 15:6): this is a figure of one who cuts themselves off from the living relationship with Christ and thus becomes incapable of bearing fruit.
G3583.origine: The Greek word comes from the adjective "xéros" (dry, arid). It regularly translates the Hebrew "yabesh" which evokes the absence of vital water, especially in the context of the desert. The root evokes the idea of life withdrawing: a plant that dries, a source that runs dry. All these uses share the image of drying as a loss of what gives life and flexibility.
G3583.emploi: This verb appears about fifteen times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels. It primarily applies to plants: seeds that dry due to lack of roots (Matthew 13:6, Mark 4:6), the cursed fig tree (Matthew 21:20, Mark 11:21), the vine branch (John 15:6). It also describes inert matter: the ripe harvest that can be harvested (Revelation 14:15) or the sea that disappears (Revelation 16:12). Applied to the human body, it evokes atrophy or stiffness (Mark 3:1, Mark 9:18). In James and Peter, it expresses the fleeting nature of human beauty in the face of the word of God (James 1:11, 1 Peter 1:24). The context changes the nuanced meaning of the word: sometimes it is death, sometimes hardening, sometimes divine judgment.
G3583.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that spiritual life needs a source, just as a plant needs water and roots. Cutting oneself off from Jesus is like a plant deprived of water: one dries up gradually and becomes barren. Conversely, remaining in Christ (John 15:6) means staying connected to the source of life. It is also an invitation to humility: our beauty and strength, like the grass of the field, dry up and disappear, while the word of God remains (1 Peter 1:24).

sens: Devoid of moisture, water
Dried up, atrophied (for the body or a limb)
Arid, barren (for the land)
Devoid of vitality, unfruitful (figurative sense)
G3584.detail:
1. The word "dry" primarily designates what has lost all moisture or water. Jesus uses it when speaking of "dry wood" that is delivered to the fire, in contrast to "green wood" still full of sap (Luke 23:31).

2. It then describes a dried and lifeless body part, unable to move — atrophy caused by illness. All four Gospels report the story of a man with a "withered hand" that Jesus heals (Matthew 12:10, Mark 3:3, Luke 6:6, Luke 6:8), and this is also how paralyzed sick people are referred to (John 5:3).

3. For the land, "dry" means arid and devoid of water — the "dry land" of Matthew 23:15 stands in contrast to the sea, referring to the dry ground where the Hebrews could walk after crossing the desert (Hebrews 11:29).

4. Figuratively, Jesus evokes "dry wood" to speak of a life without grace: if one treats green wood that still has life in this way, what will be done to dead and barren wood (Luke 23:31) — it is an image of the sinner delivered to judgment.
G3584.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that originally means "to lose moisture, to dry up." In Hebrew, it primarily translates the word יָבֵשׁ (yavèsh), which has exactly the same meaning and image: what was moist and living becomes hard and dead. It is a concrete word, drawn from the observation of nature — the fire that consumes, the sun that dries, the disease that paralyzes.
G3584.emploi: The word appears eight times in the New Testament, almost always in relation to healing or judgment. Three of the four Gospels report the miraculous healing of the man with the withered hand (Matthew, Mark, Luke), a story that shows Jesus confronting the religious hostility of the Sabbath. John uses it to describe the sick at the pool (John 5:3). Matthew also uses it for the "dry land" that the Pharisees traverse on mission (Matthew 23:15). In Hebrews 11:29, it refers to the "dry land" of the miracle at the Red Sea, a symbol of Israel's faith. Finally, Luke uses it in the image of the "dry wood" delivered to the fire of judgment (Luke 23:31), where the word carries a theological weight: the contrast between green wood (which still has life) and dry wood (barren and destined to burn).
G3584.portee: This word invites us to see in drying and paralysis the sign of sin: a life without the living water of God becomes hard, barren, dead. But Jesus comes precisely to straighten and restore — he heals the withered hand not despite the Sabbath but by magnifying it. The image of dry wood also reminds us of the urgency: without repentance, a life hardens and can only burn in judgment.

sens: Made of wood, consisting of wood
(By extension) Of little value, ordinary, without nobility
G3585.detail:
1. The word simply designates what is made of wood, the material of which an object is composed. In 2 Timothy 2:20, Paul speaks of wooden vessels in a house: these are not precious containers like those of gold or silver, but ordinary utensils made from this common material.
2. By extension, wood evokes what is common, simple, without prestige. In Revelation 9:20, wooden idols are listed alongside those made of gold, silver, and stone: they are objects of worship, but wood emphasizes their ephemeral nature and their little value compared to precious materials. The adjective then takes on a nuance of contempt: what is made of wood is fragile, perishable, unworthy of worship.
G3585.origine: The word comes from ξύλον (xylon), which means "wood" or "tree." The adjective ξύλινος adds the suffix -ινος, typical in Greek for forming material adjectives ("made of..."). In Hebrew, the corresponding word is עֵץ (etz), which designates wood and tree. This family of words is very ancient and common in both Greek and Hebrew.
G3585.emploi: The adjective ξύλινος appears only twice in the New Testament. In 2 Timothy 2:20, it characterizes vessels of lowly use in the house: Paul contrasts it with gold and silver vessels to illustrate that in the Church, there are servants of different dignities. In Revelation 9:20, wooden idols are mentioned among other materials (gold, silver, bronze, stone) that men worship: the context emphasizes the powerlessness of idols, which can neither see nor hear. In both cases, the word evokes an ordinary, accessible material, less prestigious than precious metals.
G3585.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us of two simple truths. First, that in the service of God, there are humble roles and prominent roles, and that even what seems weak or ordinary is useful to the Lord. Secondly, it warns against the worship of idols: what is made of wood or stone, perishable materials, does not deserve our worship — only God, the Eternal, deserves it.

sens: Raw material: wood
Object made of wood: stick, weapon, instrument
Stocks or wooden chains for imprisonment
Beams or gallows: the cross of Christ
Living tree with its branches and fruits
G3586.detail:
1. Wood as a raw material: it is the very substance of wood, the material that is harvested and worked. Paul speaks of it in Corinth when he refers to what endures or burns at judgment (1 Corinthians 3:12).
2. An object made of wood, notably a stick or a weapon: the guards who arrest Jesus come with "swords and sticks" (Matthew 26:47, Mark 14:48), clubs to strike with.
3. Stocks or irons: pieces of wood that confine the feet of prisoners to immobilize them. Paul and Silas endure them in prison in Philippi (Acts 16:24).
4. A beam or a gallows: in the New Testament, it almost always refers to the cross on which Jesus was executed. Peter calls it "the wood" with simple solemnity (1 Peter 2:24; Acts 5:30), as it is the instrument of our salvation.
5. A living tree with its branches and fruits: in Revelation, the tree of life in the heart of heaven produces twelve harvests of fruit (Revelation 22:2), an image of fertility and eternal life.
G3586.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and primarily designates the substance of wood, then by extension everything made from it. It regularly translates the Hebrew term עֵץ ("etz"), which means both tree and wood and wooden objects. The richness of the Hebrew word—which spans from tree to material and object—can also be found in Greek: a single word to denote the tree of the Garden of Eden, the cross, and the material that is burned.
G3586.emploi: The word appears 18 times in the provided passages, mostly in the New Testament. It primarily refers to concrete objects: the sticks of the guards who seize Jesus (Matthew, Mark, Luke), the stocks of prisoners (Acts 16:24). But its most solemn and meaningful use is for the cross: it is simply "the wood" (Acts 5:30, Galatians 3:13, 1 Peter 2:24), a bare and grave name that refers to the curse of the Law (Deuteronomy 21:22-23) and to our redemption. In Revelation, it becomes the tree of eternal life (Revelation 2:7, 22:2), a sign of final restoration.
G3586.portee: This word encapsulates a powerful Christian contrast: the "wood" of the executioners becomes the "wood" of salvation. By calling the cross simply "the wood", the early Church confessed that Jesus took upon himself the curse attached to the wood of the gallows and transformed it into an instrument of life. For the believer, this word invites us to see in every material trial—suffering, imprisonment, death—the possible place of resurrection.

sens: To cut hair very short, close to the scalp
Figuratively: to be shorn, deprived of one's hair
G3587.detail:
1. To shave means to cut hair very short, close to the head. In the Bible, it was a ritual gesture: Nazarite men would shave their heads at the end of their vow (Acts 21:24, "let them shave their heads"), an act that marked the end of their consecration to God. It was also a sign of mourning or shame.
2. Figuratively, to be shaved or to have one's hair cut meant losing one's honor, especially for a woman. In 1 Corinthians 11:5-6, Paul uses this image: a woman who prays without a veil dishonors her head "as if she were shaved", meaning she suffers a disgrace similar to that of someone whose hair has been cut. This image expresses dishonor and the breaking of an important social or spiritual rule.
G3587.origine: The verb comes from ancient Greek ξυρέω (xureō), which literally means "to shave, to cut". ξυράω is a later form. The word refers to the simple and concrete action of handling a razor (ξύρον, xyron). This action had strong symbolic significance in Israel: to shave was a ritual gesture marking either the completion of a consecration or shame or mourning.
G3587.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament, always with a strong ritual or symbolic significance. In Acts 21:24, it refers to a concrete act of purification: men under a Nazarite vow shave their heads to mark the end of their commitment to God. In 1 Corinthians 11:5-6, Paul uses it twice figuratively: being shaved or having one's hair cut becomes an image of dishonor for a woman, a supposed consequence of not respecting the veil conventions. The context shows that shaving the head was a significant and well-known gesture, used by Paul to illustrate the importance of the veil.
G3587.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, visible signs of the body—hair, clothing—carry spiritual and communal meaning. For today's believer, it invites reflection on how we honor God through our respect for the authorities He establishes, and on the coherence between our words and actions. The gesture of ritual shaving also shows that consecration to God manifests concretely in our lives.

sens: The word that designates a person, thing, or idea already known or specific (equivalent to "the" in English)
He, she, they (used alone to refer to a person)
One… the other (to distinguish two persons or groups)
G3588.detail:
1. It is the small word that Greek uses to show that one is talking about something particular, defined, that the reader or listener already knows or that the context makes clear. In English, we say "the": "The place where they were assembled shook" (Acts 4:31)—this is not just any place, it is the one where the apostles prayed together. Without this word, the sentence would refer to something vague or indefinite.
2. Sometimes, Greek uses this article alone, without a noun, to refer to a person as if pointing at them: "he" or "that one". It is like when we say "the Lord" to refer to Jesus—the word shows that we are talking about a specific person.
3. Greek also uses it to contrast two persons or two groups: "one… the other" (Galatians 4:22 recounts how one of Abraham's two women was born free and the other a slave). The article helps clarify that these are two distinct cases being compared.
G3588.origine: This article comes from an ancient demonstrative Greek word meaning "this one" or "that one", somewhat like the Latin "ille" which meant "this", "that". Over time, Greek retained this word but transformed it into a regular grammatical tool to indicate that one is talking about something specific. It is one of the oldest and most important tools in Greek grammar.
G3588.emploi: This article appears more than 7000 times in the Greek New Testament—it is one of the most frequent words in the sacred text. It is used before the names of people or things that have already been mentioned or that one wants to identify precisely: "Abraham begot Isaac" (Matthew 1:2), or "send them away, so that they may go into the countryside" (Mark 6:36). It is also found before adjectives used as nouns ("the good", "the bad"), before infinitive verbs turned into nouns, and even before entire phrases when quoting them. Its role varies according to the context: sometimes it recalls a person or thing already known, sometimes it presents it as unique or special.
G3588.portee: Understanding this article helps to read the Greek text more finely. When Jesus speaks "of the" kingdom (with the article) rather than "of a" kingdom, He shows that it is not an ordinary kingdom: it is THE promised kingdom, the unique one, the one that all await. This small distinction changes the meaning. For the Christian discovering the New Testament in the original text, grasping the article is learning to read like the first Greek readers—attentive to the nuances of the sacred text.

sens: The number 80
G3589.detail: 1. The number 80, composed of four times twenty. It is a number that Luke uses for the advanced age of Anna, the prophetess of the temple: she was eighty-four years old when she recognized Jesus as a child (Luke 2:37). It is also the number of measures of wheat that a steward must repay to his master in the parable of the unjust stewards (Luke 16:7).
G3589.origine: The Greek word comes from the ancient numbering system that counts by twenties. The root refers to the idea of multiplying four by twenty. This type of compound number was common in both classical and biblical Greek to express precise quantities.
G3589.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Luke. In Luke 2:37, it denotes Anna's age, highlighting her longevity and faithfulness in divine service throughout her life. In Luke 16:7, it quantifies a debt in an economic parable. The context is always one of precise and accounting notation, never symbolic or theological.

sens: Occupying the numerical rank of eight in a sequence
One among eight, the last of a group of eight
G3590.detail:
1. The word denotes the numerical rank of eight, the position that comes after seven in an established order. It is a simple ordinal number: "On the eighth day, they came to circumcise the child" (Luke 1:59), meaning the day that bears the number eight counting from the first.
2. By extension, the word can refer to someone who is the eighth member of a group, the last in a series of eight people. In 2 Peter 2:5, Noah is called "the eighth" because he was with seven others in the ark during the flood — Noah, his wife, his three sons, and the three wives of his sons, making a total of eight.
3. It can also designate the order in a list of objects or categories: "the eighth" of beryl in the enumeration of the twelve foundation stones of the heavenly Jerusalem (Revelation 21:20).
G3590.origine: The Greek "ogdoos" comes from a very ancient root denoting the number eight (this root is found in Indo-European). It is a simple ordinal adjective: it classifies things according to their numerical position, just as in French "huitième" contrasts with "huitain" (the whole of eight) or "huit" (the cardinal number).
G3590.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, almost always to express a precise position in a sequence: the eighth day of circumcision (Luke 1:59; Acts 7:8), the eighth among a group of eight (Noah in 2 Peter 2:5), an eighth king (Revelation 17:11), and the eighth type of precious stone (Revelation 21:20). Its meaning does not vary: it is always a numerical marker or a ranking in a series. The context of circumcision on the eighth day holds particular importance, as it was the Jewish practice prescribed by the Law.
G3590.portee: The eighth day of circumcision reminds us that obeying God in the details of daily and family life is not a marginal act, but central for a faithful believer. Noah being called "the eighth" emphasizes how, amidst a rebellious world, a righteous man can be preserved and count for God — a source of hope for those who remain faithful.

sens: What weighs, what loads and burdens
What clutters the path, what delays the race
Figuratively, an obstacle to spiritual life
G3591.detail:
1. The word ὄγκος primarily denotes a heavy mass, something bulky and heavy that weighs on you. It conveys the idea of weight, of a material burden.

2. In concrete life, it refers to what clutters, what hinders movement — like an oversized garment that impedes running (Hebrews 12:1). The image is that of a runner who must shed everything that slows him down.

3. In a spiritual and moral sense, this word designates everything that weighs us down, clutters us, and diverts us from following Christ: bad habits, worries, compromises, sin itself. It is an obstacle to perseverance in faith.
G3591.origine: The Greek ὄγκος comes from a root that evokes what is swollen, massive, bulky. The word is related to the idea of volume and weight. Paul uses it in Hebrews 12:1 to speak of the burdens that encumber us — a classic image among Stoics to describe obstacles to virtue, but taken here in a Christian sense: what hinders the spiritual race.
G3591.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 12:1. Paul uses it to urge Christians to "lay aside every weight" in order to run with perseverance. The image is that of an athlete who sheds everything that could hinder him from reaching the goal. The context shows that Paul is thinking of two kinds of obstacles: external burdens (traditions, practices) and internal sin that easily entangles us. It is a call to spiritual lightness and focus on the race of faith.
G3591.portee: This word reminds Christians that they cannot run freely in faith if they drag along unnecessary burdens — doubts, grudges, worldly attachments, or compromises with sin. The invitation is to great honesty: to identify what truly weighs us down and to cast it off to move forward toward Jesus. It is a call to lightness of heart and determination.

sens: This one, this (what is present or can be shown)
These words, this discourse (what follows)
Such, a certain (slightly indefinite)
G3592.detail:
1. The word designates a person or thing that can be seen or shown, which is there, present. It is the demonstrative of proximity: not "that distant one," but "this close one." In Luke 10:39, "She" (Jesus speaks of Mary who is before him) indicates someone concrete, identifiable.
2. Very often, the word introduces a discourse that will follow: "Here is what says" (Revelation 2:1, 2:8). The word points to the words that come, as if to say: listen carefully to these words that are coming.
3. In James 4:13, "such a city" (literally "this one or that one") designates any city, imprecise — we do not know which one, and that is the meaning: it is a light, somewhat indifferent way of speaking about a commercial destination.
G3592.origine: The word is composed of the article "the" and a small enclitic particle "de" which carries no proper meaning but reinforces and particularizes. It is a very ancient demonstrative, like the Latin "hicce" (this one precisely). It belongs to the family of Greek demonstratives, alongside "that one" and "that other." In Hebrew, similar demonstratives point to what is close to the speaker.
G3592.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Greek New Testament, mostly in Acts and Revelation. Its primary use is to mark a discourse that follows: "Here is what says" recurs constantly in the seven letters of Revelation (2:1, 2:8, 2:12, 2:18, 3:1, 3:7, 3:14), as a solemn introductory formula. In Acts 15:23, "thus conceived" uses the neuter to indicate the letter that follows word for word. Occasionally, it designates a present person (Luke 10:39) or an indeterminate thing (James 4:13, "such a city"). It is a discreet demonstrative, which does not insist like "that one"; it rather creates a proximity, an intimacy between the speaker and what he is talking about.
G3592.portee: For the Bible reader, this small word creates immediacy: when Jesus or the Spirit says "Here is what I say," we are invited to listen attentively, as if there were a living presence. The word places us before the text that follows, not as an abstraction, but as a word addressed here and now.

sens: To move from one place to another, on the way
To traverse a road, a distance
To undertake a journey
G3593.detail:
1. The verb describes the act of physically moving from one point to another, taking a road or path. It is the action of someone who is traveling, like the Samaritan in the parable who was "traveling" on the road from Jericho to Jerusalem (Luke 10:33): he was on the way, going from one place to another.
2. The word emphasizes the idea of covering a distance, progressing along a road. It can refer to both a short trip (crossing a region) and a longer journey.
3. It is a simple and concrete term for talking about the movement of a person going somewhere, without particular precision about the purpose or duration of the trip.
G3593.origine: The word comes from the noun "road" or "path" (Greek root ὁδός, hodos), to which a verbal suffix meaning "to make" is added. The basic image is therefore "to make a path," "to be on the way." In biblical Hebrew, it is primarily the verb הָלַךְ (halak, to walk) that expresses the idea; Greek translated it this way in the deuterocanonical books (Tobit 6:5, Wisdom 5:7).
G3593.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament according to its received usages, in Luke 10:33, in the famous parable of the Good Samaritan. Jesus uses it to place the action of the Samaritan: he was "traveling" on the road, meaning he was in the process of traversing the path from Jericho to Jerusalem when he found the wounded man. The context shows that this is a simple ordinary journey, interrupted by the sight of someone in distress.
G3593.portee: This verb highlights the ordinariness of the encounter with the wounded man: the Samaritan was not on a special mission; he was simply traveling. This makes his act of compassion even more striking: it is while on the way, unexpectedly, that he chose to stop and care for the wounded man. For the reader, this shows that the opportunity to show love for one's neighbor can arise at any moment, right in the midst of our ordinary journeys.

sens: To show the way to someone, to guide them step by step in their movements
To guide spiritually, instruct and teach
To orient someone towards the truth or a state of grace
G3594.detail:
1. In the most concrete sense, "to lead" means to walk in front of someone to show them the way. This is the image from the parable in Matthew 15:14: "A blind man leading a blind man" — one goes ahead, the other follows, often without true direction.

2. The word is also used for practical and immediate guidance: the eunuch asks Philip, "How can I, unless someone guides me?" (Acts 8:31), meaning: who will explain this text to me, help me understand it? Here, "to guide" means to instruct, to help step by step.

3. At a deeper level, "to lead" takes on a spiritual meaning: the Spirit of truth "will guide you into all truth" (John 16:13). This is no longer an earthly path, but a path of revelation, where God directs the soul towards divine light. Similarly, in Revelation 7:17, the Lamb "will lead" the redeemed "to the springs of the waters of life" — he guides them to the very heart of eternal life.
G3594.origine: The word comes from the Greek "hodós" (ὁδός, the way) and "hègéomai" (ἡγέομαι, to lead, to direct): literally, "to lead on the way." It is a word of service and responsibility. In the Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew verb "nachaḥ" (נוּחַ), which also means to guide, to lead with care. The word always evokes an active presence: one does not lead from afar; one walks with those they guide.
G3594.emploi: The verb appears five times in the New Testament, always with the idea of personal and responsible guidance. Three usages concern blind people leading others (Matthew 15:14 and Luke 6:39, the same saying reported twice), where the contrast is ironic: how could one who cannot see show the way? Two usages elevate the meaning to the spiritual level: the eunuch seeks someone to "guide" him in his understanding of the prophet (Acts 8:31), and especially the Holy Spirit "leads" believers into all truth (John 16:13). In Revelation 7:17, the same verb describes the Lamb guiding the redeemed to the eternal source. The word always emphasizes a living relationship, a presence that accompanies.
G3594.portee: This word invites the Christian to two meditations. First, on spiritual blindness: are we sure we see clearly, or are we leading others into emptiness without having the light ourselves? Secondly, on the guidance of the Spirit: it is the Comforter who "leads" us into truth, not our own impressions. It also calls for trust: just as the Lamb "leads" his redeemed, the believer can surrender to this divine direction and find in it the very source of life.

sens: One who guides, who shows the way to someone
One who directs, who commands others
One who leads spiritually or morally, especially referring to a teacher or a religious leader
G3595.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: a leader is one who walks ahead to show the way to others, like a guide on a journey. The word evokes the idea of directing someone on a physical road.
2. In a figurative sense, it refers to one who directs or commands within a group, who makes decisions and leads others in their wake. Judas, in Acts 1:16, is called "the guide of those who seized Jesus": he led them to Jesus to betray him.
3. By extension, it refers to one who instructs morally or spiritually, one in whom trust is placed to know how to live. In Romans 2:19, Paul ironically speaks of the Jew who is proud of himself as the "leader of the blind": he claims to be the master who teaches others. Matthew 23:16 and 23:24 show Jesus denouncing the "blind leaders" among the religious leaders: men who are supposed to lead the people but who, themselves spiritually lost, lead those who follow them astray.
G3595.origine: The Greek word comes from the union of "hodos" (the way, the road) and a root related to "hegeomai" (to lead, to guide, to direct). It literally means "one who holds the road." The root evokes the ancient idea of a chief who walks ahead, showing by his example the path to follow.
G3595.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament. Two usages are literal or nearly literal: in Matthew 15:14, in the parable of the blind, the leader is one who guides physically. In Acts 1:16, Judas is the leader who led the soldiers to Jesus. Three usages are figurative: in Romans 2:19 and Matthew 23:16 and 23:24, the word refers to the Jewish religious leaders, particularly the Pharisees. The irony of Jesus and Paul is sharp: these men claim to lead the people toward wisdom and justice, but they are "blind," meaning spiritually lost. Whoever follows a blind person will fall with him.
G3595.portee: This word reminds the Christian of the importance of discerning whom they follow. Do not blindly imitate religious leaders or teachers simply because they have a title or position: examine whether their life and teaching align with the Word of God. It is also a warning: one who proposes to lead others must first be rightly guided by the Spirit; otherwise, they will lead others into error.

sens: To move from one place to another by covering a distance
To walk or travel along a road
G3596.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of traveling, setting out, and covering a path, often a long distance. In Acts 10:9, it refers to the journey that Peter and his companions make to Caesarea: "as they were on their way" indicates that they are in the process of moving, engaged in their journey.
2. The word more broadly evokes the idea of walking, of physically progressing from one place to another. It is the concrete action of walking and earthly travel.
G3596.origine: The Greek word ὁδοιπορέω is formed from ὁδοιπόρος ("traveler," "one who travels the road"), which is itself composed of ὁδός ("road," "way") and a root related to the journey. The corresponding Hebrew word is often דרך ("way") or ארח ("to travel"), which are found in the same contexts of movement in the Old Testament.
G3596.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 10:9. It designates the journey that Peter and his companions undertake to Caesarea to meet the centurion Cornelius. Although rare in the Greek text of the New Testament, this verb belongs to the family of words related to travel and movement, common in biblical accounts of journeys and missions.
G3596.portee: This word reminds us that the apostles did not remain stationary: they moved to obey God's call and proclaim the Gospel. Peter's journey to Cornelius is a pivotal moment where the Holy Spirit expands the apostolic ministry beyond the Jews. Seeing an apostle "on the way" invites us to reflect on our own commitment to follow Christ, even when it requires us to take action.

sens: Movement from one place to another, especially on foot or by road
Journey involving fatigue and dangers
G3597.detail:
1. The journey is a movement from one place to another, often long and laborious. Jesus, "tired from the journey" near Jacob's well (John 4:6), walked for a long time under the sun to cross Samaria: the word evokes this accumulated physical fatigue along the way.
2. The journey can also refer to all the perils and dangers encountered along the way. Paul enumerates his tribulations: "Frequent journeys, I have been in danger from rivers, in danger from robbers" (2 Corinthians 11:26). Here, the word encompasses all the risks of travel—dangerous rivers, thieves, enemies—that threatened the apostle.
G3597.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek "hodos" (way, road) and "poria" (the act of going, journey). It is a compound that literally means "going by the way." The family of these words always evokes the idea of movement, of traveling a road or distance.
G3597.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Greek New Testament. In John, it refers to the physical fatigue of Jesus' earthly journey. In Paul, it extends to the sense of trials and dangers that mark the apostle's path: the traveler is never safe, exposed to nature (rivers), to humans (robbers, national enemies, false brothers), and to the sea. Paul thus makes the word a symbol of the troubled missionary life.
G3597.portee: For the Christian reader, these two uses remind us that following Jesus or serving the Gospel is never comfortable. Jesus himself experienced the fatigue of the journey, which makes his compassion for our weaknesses concrete and real. And Paul's list of trials invites the believer to see in the difficulties of serving God not an anomaly, but the normal state of the disciple: the narrow path requires perseverance.

sens: Physical passage or route allowing one to go from one place to another
Step or progression in a journey
Way of acting or living, set of principles and convictions
Religious direction or particular teaching
Means of access or approach to something or someone
G3598.detail:
1. The way is primarily a road, a concrete path: Bartimaeus is sitting by the roadside in Jericho (Mark 10:46), the seeds fall along the path (Matthew 13:4). The word also designates a direction to follow, as when the Magi return to their country by another way (Matthew 2:12).
2. A way is also a journey in progress: when one wonders what path to take, it is to seek one's route (Luke 5:19), or to continue one's journey after a meeting (Acts 8:39).
3. Figuratively, the way becomes the manner of living, behavior: the way of righteousness of John (Matthew 21:32), the way of the Cainites or Balaam (Jude 11, 2 Peter 2:15)—these are life choices that one imitates or rejects.
4. In Acts, "the way" refers to the Christian teaching itself: it speaks of "the way" as a new religious direction (Acts 9:2, 19:9, 24:22).
5. In John 14:6, Jesus states: "I am the way"—he presents himself as the passage, the personal access to the Father, condensing all the previous meanings.
G3598.origine: The Greek word hodos comes from an Indo-European root meaning "to go" or "to advance." In Hebrew, the corresponding word derech (דרך) has exactly the same semantic field: physical way and way of life. The Greek Bible (Septuagint) regularly translates derech as hodos, which explains why the Greek word can easily shift from the concrete to the figurative. The image is one of movement, of progression: one can only advance if one has a way.
G3598.emploi: The word hodos appears 99 times in the New Testament, with particular frequency in the Gospels and Acts. In its concrete senses, it designates the paths traveled by Jesus and his disciples (Mark 8:27, Luke 2:44), the places where crowds gather (Matthew 20:30). But as early as Matthew and Mark, the figurative sense emerges: preparing the way of the Lord (Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3, borrowing from Isaiah). In Acts, after Pentecost, the way clearly becomes the new Christian faith (Acts 9:2, 19:23). In Paul and James, it designates conduct, the moral or spiritual guiding line (1 Corinthians 4:17, James 1:8). The evolution is constant: from the way one travels to the way one follows, from the foot to the soul.
G3598.portee: For the Christian, this word unites the concrete and the spiritual. Physically, the way reminds us that faith is not abstract: the disciples follow Jesus, they walk with him, they learn along the way. Spiritually, it invites us to recognize that the Christian life is a chosen direction, a path to travel, not an immediate destination. Jesus' word in John 14:6 transforms everything: it is no longer just a way to find, but a person to follow. It is a call to decision, to movement, to commitment.

sens: Hard part of the mouth used for biting and chewing
Grinding of teeth, a sign of rage or extreme suffering
In a law of retaliation, equivalent to the damage received
G3599.detail:
1. The tooth is the white, hard organ implanted in the jaws, used for biting and grinding. Mark 9:18 describes a demon-possessed person whose jaw was clenched, with grinding of teeth: this is the physical symptom of terrible possession. Revelation 9:8 speaks of the locusts from the abyss having teeth like lions, an image of destructive power.
2. The grinding of teeth signifies a reaction of rage, pain, or extreme despair. Matthew 8:12 and the parallel passages (13:42, 13:50, 22:13, 24:51, 25:30) associate this grinding with weeping, depicting eternal suffering: "weeping and gnashing of teeth" in the darkness. Luke 13:28 and Acts 7:54 also show this rage expressed through the grinding of teeth.
3. In the law of retaliation, "tooth for tooth" (Matthew 5:38) means that the punishment must be proportional to the damage caused: one who has broken a tooth receives the same penalty.
G3599.origine: The Greek word ὀδούς comes from a common Indo-European root found in many languages to denote tooth. It corresponds to the Hebrew שֵׁן (shèn). The plural ὀδόντες frequently appears in passages concerning the grinding of teeth, a classic biblical image of suffering or rage.
G3599.emploi: The word appears about 12 times in the New Testament. Matthew primarily uses it in the plural in the expression "gnashing of teeth" (ὀ βρυγμὸς τῶν ὀδόντων), a recurring image of divine judgment and exclusion from the kingdom (8:12, 13:42, 13:50, 22:13, 24:51, 25:30). Mark 9:18 and Acts 7:54 describe the grinding as a sign of demonic possession or rage. Revelation 9:8 uses the word to describe eschatological creatures. The law of retaliation (Matthew 5:38) refers to it in the singular, in a legal rather than physical sense.
G3599.portee: The image of grinding of teeth in judgment calls the reader to take seriously the reality of eternal condemnation and the necessity of repentance. The expression "tooth for tooth" also reminds that Jesus goes beyond the simple application of this law: he calls to love one's enemies and to forgive without limit, revealing that true justice is that of mercy.
